#9191. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.

#9190. Vienna Actionism Museum to Cease Exhibition Program Following Controversial Otto Muehl Show

The Vienna Actionism Museum will end its exhibition program in 2027 and transition into a research institution dedicated to the transgressive postwar art movement, Monopol reports. The research institution will be open to the public by appointment only.

The privately owned institution has been a controversial presence in Austria’s art scene since opening in 2024, owing to its focus on a movement known for violent, visceral performances that often used blood and excrement as materials. But public discontent escalated into outrage earlier this year, after the museum announced that its fall exhibition would be dedicated to the work of prominent Actionist Otto Muehl, who was convicted in 1991 of crimes including the sexual abuse of minors living in a commune he led throughout the 1970s and ’80s. The show opened on September 10 and will be on view through January 10, 2027. Related Articles Otto Muehl Retrospective at Vienna Actionism Museum Courts Controversy in Advance of September Opening Inside Outsider

Muehl reentered the art scene with apparent ease after his release in 1997, receiving exhibitions at prominent Viennese institutions, including the Museum of Applied Arts, the Leopold Museum, and the gallery W&K – Wienerroither & Kohlbacher. His market surged after his death in 2014, with his works continuing to fetch six-figure prices at galleries and auction houses throughout the 2010s, according to the Artnet Price Database.

This year made clear that Muehl’s legacy was no longer so easily defended. The Vienna Actionism Museum’s exhibition, titled “Otto Muehl: Art at the Abyss,” reignited debate in Austria over the presentation of his work, particularly after several living survivors of the commune spoke out against the show. Mathilda, a group led by former commune members, called on the institution financially divest from Muehl’s work, and on the Austrian government to investigate how the commune functioned with impunity for nearly two decades. In September, protesters organized under Mathilda gathered outside the museum, displaying large banners bearing the German phrases “Pedophile criminal and cult leader” and “Perpetrator’s museum.”

Despite the backlash, the museum appeared to stand by the exhibition. “Otto Muehl is one of the major figures of Austrian, European postwar art,” Klaus Albrecht Schroeder, the show’s curator and the director of the Vienna Actionism Museum, told the New York Times. “Talking about Muehl’s artistic importance doesn’t diminish the gravity of his crimes, and acknowledging his crimes doesn’t erase his place in art history.”

Muehl’s performances, spanning the 1960s through his arrest in 1990, are documented in photographs that capture the hallmarks of his practice: nudity, violence, and provocation. Like many of his Actionist peers, Muehl frequently staged group performances. Over time, however, his artistic practice became inextricably entangled with the criminal activity at the commune, raising difficult ethical questions about how his work should be studied and the complicity involved in its continued sale.

Ruth Bourgogne, a former commune member, has said that Muehl’s series of paintings known as “Rutschbilder,” or “Sliding Pictures,” were made by painting on the bodies of girls he had sexually abused and dragging them across the canvas. “The pictures look beautiful, but they are horrific; you can’t see the suffering on their faces, but it’s inside them,” she said during a public debate at the Vienna Festival last year. Another former commune member, who remained anonymous, recounted being sexually abused from the age of three. A nude photograph taken of her when she was 12 was later sold at a prominent Viennese auction house, a sale she described as agonizing to watch.

The “sliding” works are not included in the Vienna Actionism Museum’s exhibition, though they continue to attract interest at auction: one sold for €25,000 (roughly $29,000) in 2020. According to the museum, it only exhibited works created before the founding of the commune in 1970. The museum’s founder, art dealer Philipp Konzett acquired a trove of Muehl’s works from the Friedrichshof Cooperative, which was run by former commune members after the commune’s collapse. Museum director Julia Moebus-Puckener Activismus has defended its mission as not “glorifying perpetrators” and stated that the institution does not sell paintings.

The museum exhibited a wide range of work made by the central figures of Viennese Actionism, including Günter Brus, Hermann Nitsch, and Rudolf Schwarzkogler. Work by Muehl, however, accounted for a large part of the museum’s collection. Museum shareholders said in a statement today that the “justified moral condemnation” of Muehl now overshadows his artistic legacy, making an exhibition of his work no longer viable.

Muehl expressed regret for certain offenses in 2010, on the occasion of a major retrospective at the Leopold Museum. He struck a less contrite tone in a 2004 interview with Die Zeit, in which he characterized his convictions as “character assassination” and described the teenagers he sexually abused as “fully developed girls.”

ARTnews has contacted the museum for comment.

#9188. Monumental Equestrian Statue of Roman Emperor Once Stood in Second Century Scotland

Once part of a monumental Roman-era equestrian statue, a gilded bronze lower leg and foot found in a bog in Milsington, Scotland, in 1820 will be a highlight of a new show at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh. The artifact, which dates to approximately 140 CE, was originally thought to have been looted by Scottish tribes from a site further south. But experts new believe that it came from a sculpture erected locally by Roman conquerors.

A study of sculpture fragments from Roman Scotland has shown that imperial statuary was a feature of Roman frontier forts, making a Scottish origin for the work more likely. In addition, a new analysis by National Museums Scotland shows the bronze limb was carefully detached from its parent statue, suggesting that the monument was deliberately dismantled rather than destroyed. Related Articles Moab Petroglyphs Discovered Vandalized: 'Irreplaceable Cultural Resources' See the Official Trailer for "Dig," Amy Pohler and Michael Schur's New Comedy Series

Archaeologists now think that the statue depicted the Roman Emperor Antonius Pius, who led Rome’s second major military campaign into Scotland. Under his leadership, Roman forces built the turf Antonine Wall across what is now Scotland’s Central Belt; attacks by Caledonian tribes forced a retreat south to Hadrian’s Wall less than a generation later.

“It offers us a tantalizing glimpse into the kind of grand monuments which once stood in southern Scotland and shows the importance Pius placed on his victories in Scotland,” Fraser Hunter, the principal curator of the upcoming exhibition, “Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire,” said of the remnant. “But it begs the question: Where is the rest of the statue?”

“Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire” is at NMS in Edinburgh from 14 November to 18 April

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds

What $10,000 grows to at different rates over 30 years — the rate difference matters more than you think.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Future value (FV) is the projected worth of an investment at a specific point in the future, based on an assumed rate of growth. It answers the most practical question in investing: "If I invest this money today, what will it be worth in 10, 20, or 30 years?"

Future value calculations rest on compound interest — the principle that your returns earn their own returns over time. Albert Einstein reportedly called compound interest "the eighth wonder of the world," and while the attribution is debatable, the math is not. The difference between simple interest (returns on your original investment only) and compound interest (returns on your investment plus accumulated returns) becomes enormous over long time horizons.

The basic future value formula for a lump sum investment is:

For example, $10,000 invested at 8% for 20 years:

FV = $10,000 x (1.08)^20 = $10,000 x 4.661 = $46,610

The table reveals two critical insights. First, small differences in return rates produce massive differences over long periods — $10,000 at 6% grows to $57,435 over 30 years, while the same amount at 10% grows to $174,494. That 4-percentage-point difference triples the outcome. Second, time is the dominant variable. At 8%, your money doubles roughly every 9 years — so 30 years gives you more than three doublings, turning $10,000 into over $100,000.

Most people do not invest a single lump sum and walk away. They invest regularly — monthly or per paycheck — over decades. The future value of a series of regular contributions uses a different formula called the future value of an annuity:

Where PMT is the periodic contribution, r is the periodic rate, and n is the total number of periods.

In practice, you do not need to calculate this by hand. The insight that matters is this: regular contributions are far more powerful than most people realize because each contribution starts its own compounding clock. Your first $500 contribution compounds for the full 30 years, while your 360th contribution (at month 360) compounds for just one month — but together they build wealth that dwarfs a single lump sum.

A person investing $500 per month at 8% for 30 years accumulates $745,180 — from total contributions of only $180,000. That means $565,180, or 76% of the final balance, came from compound returns rather than your own deposits. This is the engine of wealth building.

Every future value calculation should be done twice — once in nominal terms and once in real (inflation-adjusted) terms. The nominal return is the raw number your investments earn. The real return subtracts inflation, showing you what your money will actually buy.

Historically, the S&P 500 has returned roughly 10% nominally and 7% after inflation. The difference matters enormously over long periods:

That $1.13 million in nominal terms has the purchasing power of roughly $610,000 in today's dollars — still excellent, but nearly half less than the headline number suggests. When planning for FI, always use real returns (6-7%) rather than nominal returns (9-10%) to avoid overestimating what your portfolio will actually support in retirement spending.

The Rule of 72 is the simplest and most useful mental math tool in investing. Divide 72 by your annual rate of return to estimate how many years it takes for your investment to double:

This works in reverse too. If you want to know what rate of return you need to double your money in 15 years: 72 / 15 = 4.8%. The Rule of 72 is an approximation — it is most accurate for rates between 5% and 12% — but it is remarkably precise within that range and far faster than pulling out a calculator.

The FI community uses future value calculations as the backbone of retirement planning. The process works in three steps:

The table shows how starting balance and monthly contribution interact. Notice that increasing your monthly contribution from $1,500 to $2,500 (a $1,000 increase) with a $100,000 starting balance cuts 3.5 years off your time to $1 million. This is the savings rate lever in action — the amount you save each month matters more than any other variable you control.

A common question is whether it is better to invest a lump sum now or spread contributions over time (dollar-cost averaging). The math is clear: lump sum investing wins approximately two-thirds of the time because markets trend upward over the long term. However, dollar-cost averaging reduces the psychological risk of investing a large amount right before a downturn and provides a behavioral advantage that keeps many investors on track. For most FI-seekers, the question is academic — you invest each paycheck as it arrives because you do not have a large lump sum sitting on the sidelines.

When projecting your portfolio growth for retirement planning, use real (inflation-adjusted) returns of 6-7% rather than nominal returns of 9-10%. A $1 million nominal balance in 30 years has the purchasing power of roughly $550,000 in today's dollars at 2% average inflation. Planning with real returns ensures you are targeting a portfolio that can actually support your desired spending level.

Track your actual spending for 3 months and annualize it. Multiply by 25 to get your FI number using the 4% safe withdrawal rate. If you spend $60,000 per year, your FI number is $1,500,000.

Add up all retirement accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), taxable brokerage accounts, and savings. Exclude home equity and non-liquid assets. This is your starting balance for the future value calculation.

Subtract your monthly spending from your monthly after-tax income. Include employer 401(k) match and any other automatic savings. This is your periodic contribution amount for the future value formula.

Use the future value of a lump sum plus annuity formula, or a simple online calculator, to project when your current balance plus monthly contributions will reach your FI number. Use 7% real return (after inflation) for conservative planning.

Test what happens if you increase contributions by $200/month, $500/month, or $1,000/month. Seeing the concrete impact of a savings rate increase — often shaving 2-5 years off your FI timeline — makes the trade-offs tangible and motivating.

For long-term stock market projections, use 7% for inflation-adjusted (real) returns or 10% for nominal returns based on the S&P 500 historical average. For a more conservative estimate, use 6% real. For bond-heavy portfolios, use 3-4% real. Always specify whether you are using nominal or real returns — mixing them up is one of the most common planning mistakes.

Future value calculations show what WOULD happen if returns were constant every year. In reality, markets fluctuate — you might earn 25% one year and lose 15% the next. Over 20-30 year periods, average returns tend to converge toward historical norms, making future value projections reasonably useful for planning. Treat them as directional estimates, not guarantees.

Future value asks: "What will $10,000 today be worth in 20 years?" Present value asks the reverse: "What is $50,000 in 20 years worth in today's dollars?" They use the same variables but in opposite directions. Present value is useful for evaluating whether a future payout (like a pension or annuity) is worth the cost today.

The Rule of 72 works for any compounding rate, including inflation. At 3% inflation, prices double every 24 years (72 / 3 = 24). This means $50,000 in annual spending today becomes $100,000 in 24 years in nominal terms — your purchasing power is halved if your income stays flat. This is why investing in assets that outpace inflation is essential.

For FI planning, future value is more intuitive — it tells you what your portfolio will grow to. However, the most practical approach is to calculate future value using real (after-inflation) returns. This effectively gives you a future value stated in today's purchasing power, which is what you actually need to know for spending planning.

In tax-advantaged accounts (401k, IRA, Roth IRA, HSA), your investments compound without tax drag, so the standard future value formula works directly. In taxable accounts, capital gains taxes, dividend taxes, and tax-loss harvesting all affect your real return. A rough adjustment is to reduce your assumed return by 0.5-1.0% for taxable accounts to account for ongoing tax drag.

Future value calculations are the most practical tool in the FI planner's toolkit. They turn abstract concepts like compound growth and savings rate into concrete dollar amounts and specific timelines. The key takeaways are straightforward: use 7% real returns for conservative planning, always account for inflation by using real rather than nominal returns, and remember that your monthly contribution rate has a far larger impact on the outcome than chasing an extra point or two of return. The Rule of 72 gives you instant mental math for any investment decision — how long to double, what rate you need, and how inflation erodes purchasing power. Combined with a clear FI number and a disciplined savings rate, future value projections show you exactly when financial independence becomes reality. Run the numbers, test different scenarios, and let the math motivate you to increase that monthly contribution whenever you can.

Explore all of Martin’s adventures with Van Gogh here.

Tate Britain’s exhibition Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant: Inside Bloomsbury, which opened yesterday (12 November), emphasises how early 20th-century British artists were inspired by Van Gogh.

Vanessa Bell (1879-1961) and Duncan Grant (1885-1978) lived together for more than 50 years in a very Bloomsbury fashion, each having other lovers. The Bloomsbury group, named after the London quarter where they lived in the early 20th century, began as an informal collective of progressive artists, writers and intellectuals.

As the Tate show’s curator, Thomas Kennedy, points out: “When Bell and Grant were doing new and exciting things, individuals like Van Gogh—who were creating something wildly different from other artists of the time—were very much an inspiration for them.”

Bell and Grant were both also very close to the art critic Roger Fry, who in 1910 curated the pathbreaking London exhibition Manet and the Post-Impressionists, inventing the term Post-Impressionism. This show introduced Van Gogh to a British audience.

As so often with the Bloomsbury group, sexual relationships were complex and intertwined. In 1907 Vanessa had married the art critic Clive Bell, but it was always an open marriage. Two years later she started a relationship with Duncan Grant, producing a daughter, and they then continued to live together.

Duncan Grant, however, was homosexual, having numerous lovers, including a male cousin and Vanessa’s brother. To add to the complications, Vanessa later had a brief relationship with Roger Fry. The quip about the group was that they were “living in squares [in Bloomsbury], painting in circles and loving in triangles”.

The Bloomsbury relationships may seem bewildering to outsiders, but the key point to bear in mind with the current Tate exhibition is that Bell and Grant shared a home for over 50 years. Initially they lived in London, and, from 1916, partly at Charleston farmhouse in rural Sussex.

It proved to be an enduring artistic partnership. They influenced each other, and they, in turn, were influenced by modern European artists, such as Van Gogh, along with Paul Gauguin, Paul Cezanne, Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso.

The impact of Post-Impressionism: Duncan Grant's The Mantelpiece (1914) and Vanessa Bell's Still Life on Corner of a Mantelpiece (1914)

Grant, who studied art in Paris in 1906, may have then come across the work of Van Gogh. What is more certain is that Bell discovered Van Gogh in 1909, in a group exhibition at London’s New Gallery, which included a single painting by the Dutchman. She once described it as “a lovely little Van Gogh of flowers in a jug”.

The still life had been lent by Thomas Fisher Unwin, a London publisher who, with his wife Jane, had in 1896 been the first Briton to buy a Van Gogh after the artist’s death. This was a flower still life, probably one with a black background which has always been in private collections.

Van Gogh’s Bouquet of Flowers (summer 1886)

private collection (formerly Galerie Schmit, Paris)

But what was most influential for Bell and Grant was Fry's first Post-Impressionist exhibition in 1910. Including around 30 works by Van Gogh, it was the first chance for Londoners to see more than an odd painting by the artist.

This was a heady time for the Bloomsbury group. Bell later recalled: ”That autumn of 1910 is to me a time when everything seemed springing to a new life - a time when all was a sizzle of excitement, new relationships, new ideas, different and intense emotions all seemed crowding into one’s life.”

Catalogue of the second Post-Impressionist catalogue (1912), co-designed by Bell, Grant and Fry

Bibliothèque de l'Institut National d'Histoire de l'Art, Jacques Doucet collections

In 1912 both Bell and Grant had paintings in Fry’s second Post-Impressionist exhibition. They also co-designed the catalogue with Fry, and Bell helped hang the show. This time there was only a single Van Gogh, but it was again the Fisher Unwin flower still life, which Bell had known from four years earlier.

Bell, Grant and Fry all loved the south of France, where Van Gogh had also worked, and they visited regularly from the 1920s. Fry helped a friend buy a farmhouse in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, just a few hundred metres from the asylum where Van Gogh had stayed in 1889-90. On one occasion Grant visited Bell, who had bought a house just outside Cassis, on the Mediterranean coast. Grant described the surrounding landscape as “far more extraordinary than St Remi [sic]”. Both artists were well aware of Van Gogh's connection with Provence.

How then did Van Gogh’s art inspire Bell and Grant? They never set out to simply imitate his style, but were nevertheless powerfully influenced by his work and that of the other Post-Impressionists. The two British artists began to paint with heightened colours, simplified forms and strong lines.

The links can also be seen in individual pictures. Bell’s View into a Garden (1926, Bolton Library & Museum Services) includes two empty chairs, which were probably a reflection of Van Gogh’s pair of paintings of his own chair and the armchair of Gauguin (the picture of his own chair had been bought by London’s National Gallery three years earlier, so would have been well known to Bell).

In 1911, the critic Frank Rutter described Bell’s Chrysanthemums (1920, Tate, although not in the current exhibition) as “undoubtedly influenced by Van Gogh”. Its dark background echoes the Van Gogh still life which Bell had seen some years earlier.

Decades later, in 1946, Grant wrote to Bell about visiting a Van Gogh exhibition in Copenhagen, “a splendid show”. He added: “I really feel that artists should resist to the death having their works reproduced in colour. It really has been the death of Van Gogh. It’s only when one sees the originals that one realises what a very lovely & personal colour sense he had… I really do not believe in his madness as an artist at all.” Van Gogh remained in the minds of the couple for the rest of their lives.

Martin Bailey is a leading Van Gogh specialist and special correspondent for The Art Newspaper. He has curated exhibitions at the Barbican Art Gallery, Compton Verney/National Gallery of Scotland and Tate Britain.

Martin has written a number of bestselling books on Van Gogh’s years in France: The Sunflowers Are Mine: The Story of Van Gogh's Masterpiece (Frances Lincoln 2013, UK and US), Studio of the South: Van Gogh in Provence (Frances Lincoln 2016, UK and US), Starry Night: Van Gogh at the Asylum (White Lion Publishing 2018, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale: Auvers and the Artist’s Rise to Fame (Frances Lincoln 2021, UK and US). The Sunflowers are Mine (2024, UK and US) and Van Gogh’s Finale (2024, UK and US) are also now available in a more compact paperback format.

His other recent books include Living with Vincent van Gogh: The Homes & Landscapes that shaped the Artist (White Lion Publishing 2019, UK and US), which provides an overview of the artist’s life. The Illustrated Provence Letters of Van Gogh has been reissued (Batsford 2021, UK and US). My Friend Van Gogh/Emile Bernard provides the first English translation of Bernard’s writings on Van Gogh (David Zwirner Books 2023, UKand US).

To contact Martin Bailey, please email vangogh@theartnewspaper.com

Please note that he does not undertake authentications.

Linsoul’s IEM sale is truly impressive, and I've heard (and loved) 10 of the 13.

As the 11/11 sale swings into early Black Friday discounts, I've found 13 (mainly) in-ear monitor (IEM) deals that I'd personally buy today – in fact I already own 10 of them, so I don't think you can get a stronger recommendation!

All of the below wired earphones are distributed by the IEM retailer, curator, and distributor Linsoul, and with that comes a certain guarantee of quality. Everyone I've tested from them has hit a high level of quality control, so really all you as the potential buyer have to worry about, is if the sound profile is to your taste.

As I've tried most of them, I'm going to give you my tuning impressions, plus any design and comfort highlights for each of them. Many of them feature in my list of the best IEMs under $500, and my favourite budget IEMs under $100 – so these aren't just random IEM deals, but rather a curated list of genuinely excellent options.

I were to pick only one? Considering price, sound and build quality, I would get the Kiwi Ears KE4 down from $199 to $169. It's a fantastic, modern IEM that has a best-seller since its 2024 release for very good reason.

The Kiwi Ears KE4 is the one I'd recommend to most people out of all of these IEMs. That's because it has such a deliciously detailed midrange, and loads of bass (though admittedly too much for me sometimes). For $200, it's great value, and real audiophile quality. Read my full Kiwi Ears KE4 review.

The Horizon is for those that want more detail, and can handle more treble than most IEMs. Some will find it too bright, but it's just on the right side for me. With a detailed bass and decent midrange, things may be touch lean, but they are also separated and detailed. Read my Ziigaat Horizon review.

I really like these, and especially because they're only $50 – well, $42 now! For a fun, V-shape sound signature, that's a really great price, and though things get a little fatiguing after a while with the Cadenza II's full upper mids, it's still a very good IEM for under $50. Read my Kiwi Ears Cadenza II review in full.

Now you're talking... $315 may seem like too much for many people to be spending on a pair of earphones. All I can say is, if you want the best balanced tuned IEM on the market, then this is it, and that's the price for entry. Honestly, Crin could have put the price up considerable, and I believe it's great value at the discounted price.

Like bass?! Yeah, so does HBB, and although he's made several IEMs with different brands, the Deuce is one of the most beloved. I certainly think the wads of bass bring detail as well as head-throbbing amounts. But the rest of the frequencies are well-tuned too. Definitely not for everyone, this, but it's the best basshead set I've heard yet.

This is one of my favourite IEMs to date. It's bassy and warm without losing impact in the lower end, or detail in the lower mids. There's plenty (too much?) upper treble, but I find it all very nicely balanced. It's lush, warm and musical, and I love it. Read my Xenns Tea Pro review.

This IEM is fun, fun, fun. There's plenty of bass and treble, and it is a straight down the road V-shape tuning, but there's just enough detail and richness in the midrange to bring this out of the low-brow, commercial-style fare... I think its discounted price of $250 is good for this IEM.

I haven't heard this IEM, but like I say, Linsoul promises a level of quality that makes me confident in telling you about this deal. For $65 its promised reduced treble sound like an interesting approach – it's often the opposite for cheaper IEMs. Worth a punt!

I'm really interested in the Avant, as it's the first IEM that's made from Linsoul with the Linsoul brand in the name. Remember, Linsoul makes THeiaudio, Ziigaat and Kiwi Ears – that is, a lot of the best IEMs on the market today. Can't wait to hear these.

Want a pair of warm/neutral over-ear, open-back headphones? Well the Cypher is a good option, especially if you value great quality build. I found the sound to be a little soft in my Cypher review, but I can still see it being someone's ideal all-rounder.

The Halcyon IEM is a good option for those wanting that elevated treble that brings more detail to music, and who values a very small shell size. These things are tiny! I found them comfortable enough, but at the retail price I thought the Binary EP 321 were a better option. At the new sale price of $220, I think they're worth considering. #9183. Should I Exercise with a Phlegmy Cough? What You Need to Know

You’re feeling a bit under the weather, but you don’t want to lose the momentum of your fitness routine. So, should you push through and hit the gym, or is it better to rest and let your body heal? Let’s break it down!

Sleep is the best way to help your body recover quickly when you’re sick. But if you’re determined to rise and grind, you could use the “neck check” to decide whether to lace up those sneakers or stay in bed.

Many sports doctors use this theory to say that if your symptoms are above the neck — sniffles, sore throat, or a mild headache — you’re generally good to go for a light workout. But if you’re dealing with chest congestion, a hacking or juicy cough, diarrhea, a fever, or an upset stomach, it’s better to take some time to catch up on your Netflix watchlist.

Big disclaimer: there’s little scientific evidence behind the “neck check,” so use your best judgment.

If you’re going with the above-the-neck rule, exercising with the following symptoms is probably okay.

Going super hard if you have a mild cold is not a good idea. But a light workout, like a walk or a chill Peloton sesh, can be a great way to stay active without overdoing it. Stretching or light yoga might also do the trick.

Stick to light activities like walking for most earaches. Avoid intense workouts like weightlifting, yoga, or pilates, as they can throw off your balance and put pressure on your sinuses, exacerbating the pain.

Light and short workouts are likely fine if your sore throat is mild and lacks fever, cough, or swallowing issues. Remember to stay hydrated — it can ease your sore throat and is beneficial during exercise.

Light activities like brisk walks or gentle bike rides can help for allergy-related stuffy noses. If your nose is blocked, stick to very light activities, focusing on breathing. Skip workouts if you have a fever, chest congestion, or a productive cough with phlegm until you’re symptom-free.

If you’re experiencing the following symptoms, the workout can wait.

Working out with a fever increases dehydration risk and can worsen the fever. Plus, fever saps your muscle strength and coordination, making you more prone to injuries. So, do yourself a favor and skip the workout until you’re back to normal.

An occasional cough is your body’s way of clearing out irritants, but a frequent or phlegmy cough could signal a respiratory infection like a cold, flu, or even pneumonia or asthma. While a tickle-induced cough isn’t a gym deal-breaker, a persistent one is.

Diarrhea and vomiting can dehydrate you, and physical activity only makes that dehydration worse. Feeling weak? That’s a recipe for injury. Plus, stomach bugs are highly contagious. If you feel antsy, stick to light stretching or yoga at home.

The flu hits your respiratory system hard, with symptoms like fever, chills, sore throat, body aches, fatigue, headache, cough, and congestion. If you’ve got the flu, take it easy and give your body some well-earned R&R.

Once symptom-free, ease back into exercise gradually. Start with less intense workouts to avoid overdoing it. As your symptoms fade, you can gradually return to normal activity.

Regular exercise may shorten recovery time, particularly for acute respiratory infections. Listen to your body’s signals to gauge your strength. If you’re still contagious, opt for home or outdoor workouts, so you don’t spread those germs to fellow gym-goers.

P.S. Check in with a healthcare provider if you’re unsure when it’s safe to start exercising again.

#9182. Lorna Simpson Wins $105,000 Wolfgang Hahn Prize

American artist Lorna Simpson, who pioneered a new approach to conceptual photography, has been named the winner of the 2027 Wolfgang Hahn Prize. The Museum Ludwig in Cologne, Germany, which sponsors the annual prize, will put €100,000 (about $105,000) toward the acquisition of a work by Simpson for its collection. A solo exhibition of her work will staged by the institution next year, accompanied by a publication.

The 2027 award jury comprised Naomi Beckwith, deputy director and chief curator of the Guggenheim Museum in New York, and artistic director of documenta 16, and the Museum Ludwig board. Related Articles Francis Alÿs to Receive $100,000 after Winning One of the World's Biggest Art Prizes Frank Bowling Wins Museum Ludwig's Wolfgang Hahn Prize

Born in Brooklyn, Simpson rose to international renown in the 1990s with multilayered photographs that pair images with fragmented text. Her practice eventually expanded to encompass film, painting, drawing, and sculpture, often blending the boundaries between mediums while remaining focused on inner worlds and popular perceptions of Black women.

Her two-part photo-text work ID (1990) was included in Museum Ludwig’s 1999 group exhibition “Art Worlds in Dialogue (Kunstwelten im Dialog).” In that work, Simpson paired two portraits of a Black woman. In one, she turns her back to the camera; a plaque bearing the word “identity” is mounted alongside the image. The other reveals only the crown of her head, which resembles the Earth emerging from deep space. A plaque engraved with the word “identify” is mounted over this image. The museum’s catalog text from 1999 compared ID to the Black Madonna of Cologne, a famous wooden statute and site of pilgrimage housed in a 17th-century church near the institution.

“Her multifaceted body of work will provide, in the jury’s view, an important impetus for the Museum Ludwig’s collection of American art,” the museum said in a statement.

The statement continued that the acquisition “will further develop the positions in Pop Art and its use of media-influenced imagery, which Peter and Irene Ludwig acquired early on and in considerable depth.” The museum described Simpson’s work as “a bridge” to the practices of Diamond Stingily and Carolyn Lazard, whose works newly entered its collection through the Junger Ankauf initiative and “reflect on the self-image of African American women.”

Established in 1994, the Wolfgang Hahn Prize honors established contemporary artists with internationally recognized bodies of work who are not yet widely known in Germany. Previous recipients include Lee Ufan, Francis Alÿs, Kerry James Marshall, Betye Saar, Frank Bowling, and Haegue Yang.

After Jensen Huang’s resignation, maybe it's time for the company to finally rebrand.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Today, the Nvidia logo is recognised not only by dedicated gamers and creatives interested in the best graphics cards for video editing. The company's stock performance has turned it into a household name, while the demand for computer components amid the AI boom has ensured that a new headline is never far away.

Alas, it turns out that the DLSS 5 controversy is the least of its problems. Former CEO Jensen Huang has now resigned after embroiling Nvidia in a honeytrap scandal worthy of a spy novel. CFO Colette Kress has stepped up as interim CEO and an executive search has begun.

But the debacle has also resurfaced another question. Why does one of the world's most valuable companies still have such a terrible logo design? And could this be the moment for a refresh?

See our guides to the best laptops for graphic design and the best monitors for graphics artists if you need new tools for your own work.

Over on Reddit, designers are debating the "least aesthetically pleasing, most poorly designed corporate logo" still in use today, and the Nvidia logo is the example that was used to get the ball rolling. Other contenders put forward on the thread include the X logo and, of course, the infamous Kia logo.

I can see where the OP is coming from. Nvidia was the world's most valuable company until the Jensen Huang honeytrap controversy hammered its share price and put Apple back in the lead on the Nasdaq. The identities of those two companies couldn't look or feel more different. The Apple logo is sleek and minimalist. It feels modern and premium. The Nvidia logo is... weird.

"So many things I hate about this design: The Aztec-looking spiral eye, the half inverted color, the lime green, black, and white color pallette, the '80s sci-fi font. None of it coheres well," the OP writes on Reddit.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Of course, Apple and Nvidia are very different beasts. Apple is mainly consumer facing and Nvidia's business is mainly corporate. On the consumer side, Nvidia's GPUs are packaged and sold by other brands rather than by Nvidia directly. But the company is becoming much more of a household name as its tentacles spread.

Nvidia components are being promoted more visibly in GeForce RTX laptops, and the company's being collaborating on workflow developments with creative software developers like Adobe, Blackmagic (DaVinci Resolve) and the Blender Foundation.

There is a compelling case for a change. Nvidia's visual identity was born in a very different age of technology back in 1993. Its last logo redesign was twenty years ago in 2006.

Time alone is never a reason for a rebrand, even for a tech company. IBM's had the same logo since 1972. But with Nvidia, the age shows. The wonky eye, brat green colour palette and retro-futuristic type feel rooted in the late 1990s and early 2000s, when aggressive, futuristic aesthetics dominated PC hardware branding.

Compared with the cleaner, more restrained identities of companies like Apple, Microsoft, OpenAI and even AMD, Nvidia's main rival in the GPU space, the branding feels tied to gaming origins.

There's also a somewhat dark occult reference going on. In the company's name, the 'NV' comes from the shorthand that was used to identify the 'next version' in file names, while the 'invidia' part means 'envy' in Latin.

That feeling will be familiar to anyone who has a colleague with an RTX 5090, but it's a strange choice for a brand. The word is often associated with malice and the 'evil eye' and was sometimes used as the Roman name for the ancient Greek deity, Nemesis, the personification of divine retribution. Yikes.

Today, the firm's influence and ambitions extend far beyond GeForce. It sells AI infrastructure, networking technology, autonomous vehicle platforms and enterprise computing systems. A more refined visual identity could reflect its status as a global AI platform rather than a 'mere' component manufacturer.

That said, for all of its weirdness, Nvidia's mysterious green eye is one of the most distinctive marks in tech. A rebrand could risk of abandoning something that has aged better than critics might admit.

While the eye doesn't feel especially contemporary, it is unique. At a time when many companies are converging towards minimalist sans-serif wordmarks and simplified geometric symbols, the identity stands out precisely because it has character, and distinctiveness is arguably more valuable than modernity.

The strongest argument would probably be for a careful evolution. The company could modernise the typography and tweak the eye. It might be able to find a more appealing shade of green. A relatively subtle refresh could preserve decades of recognition while signalling that Nvidia has entered a new chapter.

But it remains to be seen how much the last two weeks have changed things. It looked like Jensen Huang was going to hang on until yesterday's resignation announcement. The company might also decide that the controversy requires a clear visual break from the past.

There's plenty of branding inspiration about this week that Nvidia might want to check out, from the solid Caixa rebrand in Brazil to the intriguing new Takara Tomy logo .

Let me know below if you agree that Nvidia has the worst corporate logo in tech, or if you feel that there's a stronger candidate.

#9180. MoMA Shells Out $200,000 for Inaugural Ambasz Prize for ‘Nature-Reconciled’ Architecture, Half of Which Will Go To Plant Trees

As experts gather in Antalya, Turkey for the United Nations COP31 climate change conference, the nonprofit Climate Action Tracker is warning of devastating warming by 2100, and the EU reports that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement, notes Inside Climate News.

Against this grim backdrop, New York’s Museum of Modern Art is announcing that it will give an annual grant totaling $200,000 in recognition of a single project by architects whose work is, as the award name has it, “nature-reconciled.” The prize comes with a $100,000 cash purse for the winner; it also includes another $100,000 that will go to a nonprofit organization to plant trees in the project client’s name. The prize is named the Ambasz-MoMA prize in return for a major gift from the Legacy Emilio Ambasz Foundation. It will recognize projects created anywhere in the world in the last three decades that “repair architecture’s relationship with nature,” as the museum puts it in press materials. Related Articles Zohran Mamdani Visited MoMA's West African Modern Architecture Survey and Loved It MoMA, Centre Pompidou, and M+ Will Treat Their Holdings as One Collection in Unprecedented Alliance

The museum bills it as the largest award for a single project in the field of architecture. The $100,000 cash component equals that of the Pritzker Architecture Prize, which honors living architects for significant achievement. The full $200,000 award equals the Driehaus Prize, given annually by the University of Notre Dame to a living architect working in traditional and classical architectural forms.

An Argentinian-American architect, Ambasz has had a longstanding relationship with the museum, having served as a curator in the architecture and design department between 1968 and 1976. He has contributed over $20 million total to the museum, and has served on its International Council since 1978; he served on the board of directors at MoMA PS1 from 2002 to 2006. He has won architecture awards, including one for the Grand Rapids Art Museum in Michigan.

In the inaugural year, Kashef Chowdhury/URBANA, an architecture firm based in Dhaka, Bangladesh, takes home the prize for its Friendship Centre, in Gaibandha, Bangladesh. Designed between 2008 and 2010 and completed in 2011, it is a training facility and meeting space for “underserved communities” in the flood-prone rural Jamuna River delta, which is also susceptible to earthquakes.

As the soil there cannot bear large weights, which would otherwise necessitate costly elevated foundations, the Friendship Centre instead employs a compacted earthen embankment to protect it from floods. It was built by hand almost exclusively with clay bricks made locally by area workers. Its form and style were inspired partly by the ruins of a monastery at nearby Mahasthangarh, the earliest known archaeological site and oldest city in the country, dating back to at least the third century BCE.

“The Friendship Centre has been in service to an underserved community for 14 years. Yet, it is not a building of 14 years of age, but rather 2,300 years of age, as it draws its inspiration for flood protection from the nearby third-century BC settlement of Mahasthan,” said Chowdhury in press materials. “We are delighted that its coexistence with the surrounding agricultural, rural landscape, without really showing its mass forms to adjoining villages, has been recognized in this important judgment.” Chowdhury established his firm in partnership with Marina Tabassum in 1995 and has been principal since 2005. He was the Aga Khan Award for Architecture for the Friendship Centre in the 2014–16 cycle, as well as qualifying as a finalist for the same award in 2004 for A5, a pavilion apartment.

The Centre, which includes offices, classrooms, a library, meditation spaces, dormitories, and dining facilities. It also employs green roofs, open-air courtyards, and interconnected rainwater harvesting pools to moderate temperatures and provide natural ventilation. Mean temperatures can range into the mid-90s in April and May, with relative humidity averaging between 65 and 74 percent.

The other $100,000 will go to the Fundación Gran Chaco in Formosa, Argentina, which will contribute to reforestation efforts in the Gran Chaco forest in honor of Friendship, the NGO founded and directed by Runa Khan, who commissioned the Friendship Centre.

The Friendship Centre was chosen from a pool of nearly 140 projects, developed through research by the Ambasz Institute along with nominations by 30 international experts nominating candidates from their own regions.

The Emilio Ambasz Institute for the Joint Study of the Built and Natural Environment was established in 2020 and is housed in MoMA’s department of architecture and design. It organized the 2023–24 exhibition “Emerging Ecologies: Architecture and the Rise of Environmentalism.” e-flux wrote that “the exhibition imagines an alternative American future where nature is in harmony with human settlement—technologically, aesthetically, and spiritually,” and called it “a brilliant cross-section of architectural innovations as they were developed.”

“This inaugural prize marks an important extension of the Institute’s research beyond the Museum, recognizing exemplary architectural practice while supporting tangible environmental action,” said Evangelos Kotsioris, director of the Emilio Ambasz Institute and an architecture and design curator at MoMA, in press materials. “By honoring Kashef Chowdhury/URBANA’s extraordinary work on the Friendship Centre, the inaugural Ambasz–MoMA Prize recognizes an architecture that brings together environmental adaptation, historical continuity, and an extraordinary sensitivity to the communities it serves.”

Serving on the inaugural prize jury along with Kotsioris were Martino Stierli, chief curator of architecture and design, and Paula Vilaplana de Miguel, assistant curator of architecture and design. Two distinguished external jury members—Shelley McNamara, of Ireland’s Grafton Architects and Wang Shu, of China’s Amateur Architecture Studio—joined the museum’s jury.

#9179. Does Creatine Increase DHT? What You Need to Know

Ah, creatine! It’s a popular supplement promising muscle gains and enhanced performance. But as you’re hitting the gym harder and seeing results, there are some potential side effects to be aware of. Here’s the lowdown.

Creatine monohydrate is a naturally occurring substance found in muscle cells. It helps to produce adenosine triphosphate (ATP) — your muscles’ go-to fuel when working hard.

Although you can find creatine in foods like red meat and seafood, many gym enthusiasts and athletes boost their stores with supplements. Why? Because more creatine equals more ATP, which means more energy for high-intensity activities. More fuel means more mileage!

Now, here’s where things get hairy. You might dial up your body’s DHT (dihydrotestosterone) production when you uplevel creatine. DHT is a derivative of testosterone and plays a big-league role in developing male characteristics. But here’s the catch: while DHT might beef up your alpha vibe, it’s also notorious for thinning out hairlines in peeps predisposed to male pattern baldness.

So, do creatine supplements cause baldness? Maybe! The buzz mainly stems from a small 2009 study where college-aged rugby players loaded up on creatine and saw their DHT levels increase significantly.

Because DHT can shrink hair follicles and shorten the hair growth cycle, it may seem logical to blame creatine for contributing to hair thinning. However, it’s important to remember that these findings are a one-hit wonder — they haven’t been seen again in other studies. Plus, let’s not forget that intense workouts alone can pump up these hormones, too.

As a result, the jury’s still out, making the creatine-and-baldness saga a hot topic for gym gossip and scientists alike.

The same 2009 study found that after a week of taking high-dose creatinine at 25 grams per day, DHT levels rose by 56%. When the researchers dropped the dose to 5g daily for two more weeks, levels remained 40% higher than baseline. These findings contrasted with the control group participants who took a placebo.

Does this mean creatine could spell disaster for your do? Well, creatine boosts DHT, the usual suspect in male pattern baldness, also called androgenic alopecia. However, your disposition to hair loss and the effects of DHT is genetic, meaning that it’s inherited.

Some folks are more prone to DHT’s hair-ruffling effects because of how their androgen receptor gene is wired. Hormones like testosterone and DHT bind to androgen receptors, typically triggering normal hair growth. However, variations in the AR gene make the androgens extra effective, making you more likely to experience hair loss.

So, while there isn’t much evidence to say that creatine supplements cause hair loss, the connection to increased DHT levels is worth considering if your family reunions look like a convention for bald eagles.

Beyond the potential for a breezy scalp, creatine is actually solid in the safety department, with long-term studies giving it a thumbs up. However, although creatinine doesn’t pose a risk to healthy individuals, it might not be your best move if you have kidney, high blood pressure, or liver disease.

Another thing to keep in mind is that creatinine loves to hang onto water, so expect some extra bloat and weigh-in surprises as your body adjusts.

Thinking of starting a creatine kick? Chatting with your doctor first is always wise, especially if you have other health conditions or take medications. They can advise you and rule out any potential interactions.

If you’re taking creatinine and notice changes to your hair, a check-up is a good idea. Shedding a few strands is normal, but it’s a red flag if you start losing clumps of hair. Rapid hair loss can indicate underlying health issues that go beyond your hairstyle.

Furthermore, consult a doctor if hair loss is weighing on your mind. They can offer solutions or treatments to manage your hair loss and stress.

Creatine is celebrated for its muscle-building prowess, but rumors of a link with hair loss exist. The good news is there’s little conclusive evidence directly connecting creatine supplementation to permanent hair loss.

However, creatine loading may boost DHT levels, a hormone linked to male pattern baldness, especially in people genetically predisposed to hair thinning.

So, if you’re concerned about hair loss, it might be wise to talk with a doctor before adding creatine supplements to your muscle-building routine.

My latest stylised project, Iomall, was inspired by Yehliu Geopark and Seceda Mountain. Built in Unreal Engine 5, it combines Lumen and Nanite Foliage to create a stylised environment.

The landscape shader combines Global Albedo Maps, Nanite Tessellation, RVT blending, height blending and cell bombing.

To reduce texture tiling across large landscapes, I implemented cell bombing in the terrain material. This technique adds variation to repeated textures, allowing large surfaces to be covered with fewer material layers while maintaining a natural appearance.

#9177. Artnet’s Kalshi Partnership Faces Swift Backlash Online, But Advisers Are More Mixed

The art world, as much as we love it, has never been accused of lacking opportunities for speculation. But apparently “there’s room for one more, honey.“

On Wednesday, Artnet announced that it had partnered with Kalshi, the prediction-market platform that lets users bet on everything from election results to sporting events. Artnet will become Kalshi’s official art partner, helping select markets and supplying the auction data used to determine which bets pay out.

The reaction on Instagram was swift and, let’s say, not particularly kind. Related Articles Beowolff Combines Artsy and Artnet in Digital Art Market Push Artnet CEO Resigns Abruptly Before Annual General Meeting

“How convenient. Now you can misunderstand art from anywhere,” wrote one commenter.

“Listen y’all there simply weren’t enough ways to artificially inflate an artist’s market and destroy their career before they turn 30,” wrote another.

Then came perhaps the most inspired comment, which may be a prediction of Artnet’s next move on the chessboard: “UFC x ARTNET! ARTNET JOE ROGAN.”

The partnership comes seven months after Artnet, the auction-data and media company, announced a mergerwith the online art brokerage Artsy. The combined company is led by chairman Andrew Wolff, CEO of Beowolff Capital, which acquired majority stakes in both companies over the past year.

It also comes just days before New York’s marquee November sales, which will offer plenty of chances to put the partnership to the test. Kalshi introduced art-related prediction markets in May and already offers contracts on individual paintings, entire collections, and whether artists will break their auction records.

Take Yoshitomo Nara’s Candy Blue Night (2001), which is headed to Sotheby’s on November 16. Users can trade contracts on whether the painting will sell for more than $6 million or $7 million. They can also trade on major works by Francis Bacon, Andy Warhol, and Roy Lichtenstein that are coming up for sale.

For now, the money changing hands in Kalshi’s art markets is dwarfed by the value of the objects being bet on. On Thursday, a market for Sotheby’s Blaquier-Arrieta Collection showed a roughly 52 percent probability that the sale would exceed $500 million. At the time, it had attracted just $372 in trading volume.

Still, the idea of making money from an auction without having to buy anything has its attractions.

Wendy Cromwell, founder of the advisory firm Cromwell Art and a former Sotheby’s contemporary-art specialist, saw some promise in the idea but also reasons for concern.

“I do think it’s a way for people to participate in the community,” she said. She added that she meant people who are engaged with the art world, follow artists, and understand their markets, even if they aren’t collectors themselves.

But Cromwell also saw a potential problem: the advantage held by people with access to information the public doesn’t have.

“It’s going to be extraordinarily tempting for everybody because everyone in the art world has inside knowledge,” she said.

Philip Hoffman, founder and chairman of the Fine Art Group, was less enthusiastic. “I can’t see that it’s a great use to collectors,” he said. In his view, there’s no reliable way to predict the prices of major works, where personal preference, provenance, condition, and the whims of the wealthy can render even the most carefully considered valuations irrelevant.

Results for more ordinary works, he said, can be relatively predictable. The top of the market is another matter. “People get carried away if they truly want it, and there’s no price,” he said.

Hoffman recalled once guaranteeing a Willem de Kooning painting that everyone expected to fetch substantially more than $10 million. Then the stock market fell, bidders disappeared, and he was left owning the painting himself. He eventually sold it for $9.7 million, taking a $300,000 loss. In other words, even knowing who intends to bid is no guarantee of knowing what will happen when the auctioneer raises the gavel.

There are also more troubling possibilities.

The art market runs on information that isn’t always available to the public. Auction-house specialists usually know how many bidders are registered for a sale. Dealers and advisors may know who is interested in a painting, how badly they want it, and what they’re prepared to pay. Guarantors may already have a financial stake in a work before it reaches the auction block.

That’s an obvious problem for a prediction market. A casual participant might have access to auction estimates, past sales results, and whatever enthusiasm is circulating on social media. Someone closer to the sale, meanwhile, might know about confidential expressions of interest, guarantees, or the number of absentee bidders. The two would hardly be working with the same information.

Then again, access to sensitive information isn’t limited to senior specialists. Junior employees who help keep the wheels of commerce turning could also be privy to confidential bidding information, giving them an advantage over ordinary traders.

When Kalshi first moved into the art market in May, Christie’s and Phillips told ARTnews that they have robust policies governing the use of confidential information and participation in activities that present a conflict of interest. Both said those policies cover prediction markets. Sotheby’s declined to comment at the time.

For its part, Kalshi prohibits trading on material nonpublic information. Its rules for artwork-price contracts also bar certain insiders from participating, including consignors, bidders, guarantors, and auction-house employees involved in a sale. But identifying those people and enforcing those restrictions in a business built on discretion is a challenge of its own.

The question I can’t stop turning over: Could prediction markets influence the auctions themselves? One can imagine a feedback loop in which speculative enthusiasm on prediction markets drives expectations higher and sways real buyers. A collector who sees overwhelming confidence that a picture will blow past its estimate might begin to second-guess an advisor’s valuation. Dealers or other interested parties might also see an opening to stoke enthusiasm for an artist’s market.

There’s another intriguing possibility. Might collectors use prediction contracts to offset some of their auction spending, effectively hedging their exposure to a purchase? Or might they look for gaps between the expectations reflected on Kalshi and what they believe artworks will actually bring at auction?

But there’s a catch. Kalshi’s rules prohibit people who can influence an auction’s outcome from betting on it. And with so little money being wagered so far, there isn’t much to be made anyway.

For now, the gap between multimillion-dollar auctions and prediction markets with little real money on the line suggests that Kalshi’s art offerings are more experiment than alternative financial market.

Still, Artnet’s involvement adds another dimension. The company will help identify subjects for prediction markets and provide data from its Price Database to verify the outcomes. Kalshi will continue to design the contracts and operate the exchange. Artnet has said its newsroom will not be involved in creating the markets or verifying results.

For Cromwell, the important question is whether anyone should treat these predictions as a serious measure of what art is worth.

“I think it’s a fool’s game to listen to prediction markets,” she said. “If you’re spending lots and lots of money, you should do your own research and have your own convictions about what you want to spend.”

#9176. How Frieze became the latest step in Abu Dhabi's cultural masterplan

Lighting up the city: the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi, which has taken over from the Abu Dhabi Art fair, is at the Manarat Al Saadiyat cultural hub on Saadiyat Island © Department of Culture and Tourism, Abu Dhabi

Frieze Abu Dhabi (19-22 November) debuts next week to a crescendo of cultural development in the emirate. As 2026 draws to a close it brings the launch of the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, which joins three other museums in the Saadiyat Cultural District that have opened in the past 18 months. Meanwhile, the second editions of the Public Art Biennial and Nomad Abu Dhabi art and design fair take place this month, while plans continue for Miza, the creative quarter in Mina Zayed.

While most of Abu Dhabi's cultural projects are newly launched, the city’s art fair has been running under various guises for nearly 20 years. It began in 2007 as ArtParis Abu Dhabi, held first at Emirates Palace, the luxury hotel on the Corniche, before later rebrandeding to Abu Dhabi Art and moving to Manarat Al Saadiyat, where it remains today. In those early years, galleries looked towards the newly announced Saadiyat museum projects. Heavyweights such as Gagosian, White Cube and Hauser & Wirth sold works primarily by Western artists at high prices and with institutional buyers in mind. As acquisition strategies shifted in the 2010s, many of the larger galleries left Abu Dhabi Art and the fair turned towards the Arab region and the Global South.

Frieze Abu Dhabi director Dyala Nusseibeh. “It’s a marriage,” Nusseibeh says about the fair’s partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism. “And the fair is a celebration—you’re coming to the wedding” Courtesy Frieze Abu Dhabi

Regional stalwarts stayed, among them Green Art Gallery and the Third Line from Dubai, and Elmarsa from Tunisia, and it is thanks to the sustained efforts of the region's scene that art from the Arab world is gaining stature, institutional backing and international recognition. For example, the three artists on the stand of Dubai gallery Lawrie Shabibi—Mandy El-Sayegh, Shaikha Al Mazrou and Hamra Abbas—all now have international profiles. Meanwhile Dala Nasser, the inaugural winner of the Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, arrives fresh from solo shows at Nottingham Contemporary in the UK and Kunsthalle Basel in Switzerland.

This market, nonetheless, has conspicuously lagged. Art from the Arab world remains comparatively underexposed and relatively inexpensive. According to Dyala Nusseibeh, who joined Abu Dhabi Art as director in 2016 and now directs Frieze Abu Dhabi, the UAE accounted for 45% of all buyers of Mena (Middle East and North African) art in 2025. Collecting is rising among the younger Gulf generation, and the number of private collectors in Abu Dhabi has grown over the past decade, among Emiratis and foreign residents alike. Yet most Mena artists still sell to people with a connection to the region, a pattern both Frieze and the emirate are keen to break.

"We got to a point where we’d stretched as far as we could within our existing framework in building the market," Nusseibeh says. “We’re now ready for that next step outward—integrating the local and the regional market far better into the global market."

That step is a "marriage", Nusseibeh says, between the international fair giant and Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT), which ran Abu Dhabi Art. “The fair is a celebration—you’re coming to the wedding,” she says, framing the arrangement as an evolution of the fair rather than a takeover.

Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox describes the company following a growing market. “Our last new fair was in Seoul, and we just had our fifth edition, which was very successful,” he says. “We’ve been looking at how the art market is evolving, where collectors are, where there is growth. Unsurprisingly, this region is of great interest and becoming more so.”

Frieze’s offer is twofold. First, it promises greater international exposure for galleries and artists from the region, and not only through the curators and collectors it brings to Abu Dhabi. The Third Line, for example, secured a slot at No. 9 Cork Street—Frieze’s year-round London outpost—during Frieze London, on top of its place in Abu Dhabi. Second, the fair offers its regular Western galleries, facing a faltering market, entry to a new collecting cohort.

The Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, scheduled to open on 11 December, is in Abu Dhabi’s Saadiyat Cultural District Courtesy the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi

Despite Fox’s Seoul comparison, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents a different arrangement: it is a partnership with a state entity, behind which lies a web of capital and longstanding business relationships. Frieze was previously owned by Endeavor, the company run by Ari Emanuel. When Endeavor was taken private by the investment firm Silver Lake and its assets bought back in 2025, it was split into three: what Fox calls the “fighting assets”, the Ultimate Fighting Champion (UFC) and World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE), combined as TKO; the talent agency William Morris Endeavor (WME); and the live-events businesses, Frieze among them, under a new company founded by Emanuel called Mari.

Mubadala, one of Abu Dhabi’s sovereign wealth funds, is a key backer of Silver Lake, having put in $2bn in 2020 and signed a 25-year strategic co-operation agreement. Mubadala has also invested directly in Mari, as has the Abu Dhabi media group IMI. That builds on a close relationship dating to the 2010s between Emanuel and Mubadala chief executive Khaldoon Al Mubarak, the brother of DCT director-general Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak.

This multifold investment by Abu Dhabi into Frieze should mean the fair is well supported, even as its first edition takes place amid regional instability. In should also ensure Frieze's plans align closely with those for the emirate as a whole. Nonetheless, the decision to not align the opening of Guggenheim Abu Dhabi with the fair will likely mean fewer international visitors for Frieze.

Zayed National Museum opened in December 2025 Courtesy Zayed National Museum

The arrival of Frieze, and the rest of Emanuel's portfolio, chimes with Abu Dhabi’s embrace of luxury and high-end events—which is, of course, another way to describe an art fair. Mari's holdings include elite tennis, such as the Mubadala Abu Dhabi Open. The sovereign wealth fund ADQ’s $1bn investment in Sotheby’s in 2024 has produced a second year of auctions at the five-star St Regis hotel, where the auction house is selling jewellery as well as art. Next door to Manarat Al Saadiyat, the fair’s venue, sits not only the museums but the luxury Saadiyat Grove Mall, where its developer, Aldar, also chaired by Mohamed Khalifa Al Mubarak, has commissioned major works by serious artists. Emanuel has often called this the entertainment and experience ecosystem: a synergistic portfolio spanning live events, luxury and leisure.

How measurably this will touch the fair itself remains to be seen. When Endeavor, then WME-IMG, took a stake in Frieze in 2016, pundits predicted crossovers between celebrities and artists that never materialised, and WME was later reconfigured as a separate entity. Frieze maintains that it retains full creative control, although with input from DCT, and has no plans to alter the art-centred formula that has served it well.

The luxury connection matters less for the fair than for what it reveals about Abu Dhabi’s positioning as a city for global elites. The private-equity and investment firms that have been arriving at pace until Iran's missile strikes on the Gulf earlier this year tell the same story. As does the commitment to an event-driven lifestyle, with calendar points throughout the year that drive business to the emirate. This week, Frieze; next month, the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix, Abu Dhabi Collectors’ Week and Guggenheim Abu Dhabi.

Stepping back, Frieze Abu Dhabi represents one part of a longer, grander plan for the emirate. Accordingly, its success will be measured not only in sales, but whether the artists at its heart will eventually launch onto the global stage. The Guggenheim's arrival is expected to further propel Abu Dhabi's efforts to canonise not only the UAE’s contemporary scene, but also the history of Arab Modernism, which unfolded largely further west in the Maghreb, Egypt, Lebanon, Syria and Iraq.

The fair’s geography has also widened since its early editions, most notably with the growing importance of South Asian artists and collectors. Some of the most successful stands in recent years at Abu Dhabi Art have come from the subcontinent, and Frieze boasts a significant South Asian contingent, including Experimenter, Galerie Isa, Jhaveri Contemporary, Nature Morte and Project 88. South Asia shapes the non-commercial programme too: the curator Tarini Malik anchors her section, Global Futures, in the Arabian Sea, which connects South Asia and the Arabian Peninsula, and positions Abu Dhabi at the heart of a re-ordered world.

Taking over the longstanding Abu Dhabi Art, the Frieze brand has lured international dealerships alongside a strong showing of regional names

#9175. 10 Signs You Might Not Really Be in Love: How to Tell the Difference

Love can feel like navigating a choose-your-own-adventure book with half the pages missing. Are you truly in love or just caught in a wave of infatuation? Sometimes, what seems like a heart-thumping romance may be a fleeting crush.

Wondering how to tell the difference? We’ve got you! Here’s a rundown of the 10 signs you’re not really in love.

Feeling a bit puzzled about your feelings for boo? That’s pretty normal. But before you start planning your future or picking out matching Halloween costumes, you may wanna make sure it’s real love and not a case of a serious crush.

Here are some signs that you may not really be in love:

Caught up in the romance novel vibe? If you’re all about the feelings of being in love rather than who’s sharing your popcorn, it might just be that you’re smitten with the idea of love itself.

Time to check if your relationship is more about the fairy tale than the real person.

Chatting with your partner shouldn’t feel as shallow as a kiddie pool. If deep talks are tougher than pulling teeth and rarer than a unicorn, it’s a red flag.

Sticking to small talk about the weather and dinner plans suggests the emotional depth for a lasting bond might be missing.

When discussions about future plans feel as far-fetched as sci-fi adventures, they may reveal underlying doubts about the relationship’s viability.

If imagining a future together feels unrealistic or undesirable, it’s time to ask yourself why. Real love plans a future; infatuation lives for the weekend.

Remember when their sock on the floor was cute? If little quirks now make you more cranky than charmed, it might mean the love goggles are off, your feelings have shifted from affection to annoyance, and the reality check has bounced.

Love is seeing imperfections and adoring them anyway.

Feeling more at ease or more ‘yourself’ when your partner isn’t around is a telling sign. If you’re secretly throwing mini-parties when they leave the room, you need to stop and think. Real-deal love means missing their chaos when they’re gone, not celebrating the silence.

Shared values are the anchor of deep, lasting relationships. If your core values clash more than a polka dot and stripes ensemble, you’re in for a rough ride, as finding common ground could be challenging!

Lasting love grows from shared beliefs and mutual respect, not from opposing battle lines.

No respect? No future. Respect is as critical to love as air is to breathing. Without mutual respect, you might just be coexisting rather than genuinely connecting.

If you no longer admire or respect each other’s opinions and choices, sustaining a healthy relationship will be difficult.

If they’re out of sight and totally out of mind, that’s not just independence — it might be indifference. When love is real, you should long for their laugh or lame jokes when they’re away. Could it be that your emotional attachment isn’t as strong as it should be for a lasting relationship?

If your best moments are consistently away from your partner, your heart might not be in it to win it. Perhaps your relationship isn’t providing enough support or happiness.

True love enriches your life and doesn’t play second fiddle to your social circle. It’s time to evaluate where your emotional energy is invested.

Still window shopping while you’re supposedly locked down? It’s a sign you might not be all in. A love that lasts doesn’t keep a backup catalog — it’s too busy loving what it already has.

Knowing why you’re still scanning for alternatives can help you address what might be missing or unfulfilled in your relationship.

Are you genuinely in love or just in love with being in love? If you’re secretly thrilled when they’re not around, stuck in surface-level chit-chat, or dreading deep-future talks, these are cosmic signs that it’s rethink o’clock.

Don’t ignore the signals — tuning in now can save you heartache later and lead you toward a love that genuinely fulfills you.

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024
