#9110. ZAV Architects extends house in Iran with ombre "architectural limbs"

Photography by Parham Taghioff unless otherwise stated

A series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue on this home extension on the outskirts of Tehran, designed by Iranian studio ZAV Architects.

Named Golmorad, the colourful extension transforms the residence from a weekend villa, originally designed by Iranian studio Firouz Firouz, into a permanent home in the town of Kouhsar.

ZAV Architects‘ intervention extends both ends of the home into three adjacent orchard plots acquired by the client.

Constructed from masonry, the extension is coated in plaster to blend in with the earthen exterior of the original home, while its curved geometries set it apart from its predecessor.

Aiming to appear as if organically growing from the home, Golmorad emerges as a series of overlapping arched roofs.

At one end, the vaulted extension branches into two curved forms that gradually decrease in height – one wing containing a bedroom and ensuite, and the other an open-plan kitchen, living and dining room that opens onto an outdoor pool.

Openings between the overlapping roof planes let light into the home’s interior.

“Rather than approaching the extension as either a replication of the original structure or a distinctly separate addition, the project explores a third possibility: an architecture that emerges from within the existing building itself,” ZAV Architects told Dezeen.

“This intervention can be understood as a process of grafting, in which new needs and aspirations are grafted onto the existing body of the villa, giving rise to new architectural limbs that branch out and grow from it,” it continued.

“It is as though the original building, while retaining its underlying architectural logic rooted in thick-earth construction, has developed new and distinct organs of its own.”

ZAV Architects created a gradient effect across the building with terracotta tones fading into blue, intending to strengthen the appearance of the extension growing from the home.

“The uniform colour of the original villa develops into a chromatic spectrum that radiates outward from the existing core towards the newly formed branches,” the studio said.

“This transition makes the process of transformation visible, with each segmented shell expressing a distinct stage in the building’s evolution.”

Golmorad is shortlisted in the house extension category of this year’s Dezeen Awards. It recently won the awards’ public vote alongside a playground also designed by ZAV Architects.

Last year, ZAV Architects was among the winners of the Aga Khan Award for Architecture for the Majara Residence and Community Redevelopment, a colourful domed cultural retreat on the Iranian island of Hormuz.

Photography by Parham Taghioff unless otherwise stated

#9108. Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

For all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy new medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

But retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

If you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next big thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

Retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

But retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” says Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”

The medication is currently in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide users lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

In fact, this has become such an issue that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

“Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

“People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”

That includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

But compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel says. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

Dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you plan to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he says.

But, with all medications, Dr. Ali says it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

Dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

“Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle plan focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel says. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

If you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali says. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more important, he points out.

#9107. Viking legend informs ring-like viewpoint on Icelandic mountain ridge

Photography by Claudio Parada Nunes

Ring of Bjólfur is a mountain viewpoint in Iceland, designed by local studios Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking.

Located in Seyðisfjörður, a fjord in eastern Iceland, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks.

Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture‘s design draws on the legend of Bjólfur, an Icelandic Viking settler believed to have claimed this landscape and been laid to rest on the mountain.

Local lore says Bjólfur was buried on the mountain with his most precious belongings, though they have never been found. The viewpoint, therefore, evokes a ring that has been left for him.

“The medieval Book of Settlements, or Landnámabók, tells of Bjólfur, the settler who first claimed land in Seyðisfjörður and gave the mountain its name,” Arkibygg Architects told Dezeen.

“The book says little about him, but local tales tell that he was laid to rest in a burial mound high up on the mountain,” it continued.

“By ancient custom, chieftains were often buried with their treasures, silver and jewellery. Bjólfur’s grave goods have never been found, but we let our imagination run free and left him a great silver ring.”

Arkibygg Arkitektar and Esja Architecture won a competition to design Ring of Bjólfur in 2021. The project was shortlisted in the small projects category of this year’s Dezeen Awards and also won the public vote for the same category.

Ring of Bjólfur takes the form of a perfect circle, measuring 32 metres in diameter. While emulating a ring, this was also designed to “work with views in every direction”.

Positioned on a mountain ridge 650 metres above sea level, the structure was built from post-tensioned concrete with stainless steel railings, chosen for durability and for colours that emulate silver. It partially cantilevers on one side.

“The ring can be used in many ways, and the view changes depending on where you are in the circle – and whether you are standing or sitting,” said Arkibygg Arkitektar.

“The choice of materials grew from the idea of creating a silver ring, while also having to withstand wind and weather at 650 metres, with the structure being submerged in snow for parts of the year,” said the studio.

A major focus for the studios was ensuring accessibility, creating “an experience that everyone can enjoy, including wheelchair users”.

To achieve this, they designed accessible parking next to the ring as part of the project. Further general parking is located further downhill to encourage people who are physically able to walk to the platform.

“The project has been very well received, not only by visitors but just as much by local residents,” it continued.

“The ring is already strengthening tourism in the town, and it has also become part of residents’ daily lives, widely used for outdoor recreation. People walk, cycle or even ski up there to take in the view.”

The landscape surrounding the viewpoint was preserved as much as possible, with any boulders that needed to be temporarily removed lifted back into place upon completion.

“The immediate surroundings – the soil and the rocks – matter a great deal. The aim was to disturb the ground as little as possible and to repair what was disturbed.

“Other areas affected by the works were restored with native vegetation. Having one clear destination also keeps visitors from wandering across the fragile ridge.”

Other viewpoints recently featured on Dezeen include an arrow-shaped structure in Denmark by Arup and the Lech Mountain Mirror by Snøhetta in Austria.

#9106. arnaud behzadi on designing beyond beauty, from paris’ doobie’s to pavyllon lyon

the french architect discusses how memory, emotion, and hospitality shape two new restaurants, from a parisian icon to a culinary school in lyon.

Speaking with Arnaud Behzadi is something of a masterclass in understanding architecture beyond aesthetics. For the Paris-based architect, spaces are living entities, capable of provoking emotions, awakening memories, and shaping human relationships, provided they have been designed with enough sensitivity. His approach challenges the notion that beauty is something we merely observe. Instead, he believes it is something we experience, often without fully understanding why. This conviction runs through his work, from his furniture collection BAM to two of his latest hospitality projects: the reinvention of Doobie’s, an iconic Parisian restaurant, and Pavyllon Lyon, conceived in collaboration with celebrated chef Yannick Alléno. Although radically different in character and purpose, both reveal an architect determined to create places that resonate long after the first impression has faded.

For Behzadi, architecture begins with an exercise that might sound deceptively simple: listening. ‘We learn at school to listen, to hear, not so much to watch the space,’ he tells designboom, describing a process of observing materials, light, emptiness, and the sensations they produce before drawing a single line. Only then does he establish what he calls a narrative program, a conceptual thread that informs every subsequent decision. This philosophy finds an especially personal expression at Doobie’s, located at 26 Rue Marbeuf in Paris’ eighth arrondissement. Founded in 1938, the establishment became a fixture of Parisian nightlife in the 1990s, a place Behzadi himself remembers from his younger years. Following three years of transformation, the architect has given it a second life without attempting to erase its first. ‘What I remember more than everything was the energy of this place,’ he recalls. ‘I was really feeling that I was being hosted, that I was home, not that I was being served.’

Rather than designing another fashionable restaurant, Behzadi drew inspiration from the tradition of Parisian private dinners, where artists, politicians, writers, and intellectuals would gather around the same table. He studied the domestic worlds of figures such as the Agnellis, François Catroux, and Yves Saint Laurent and Pierre Bergé, imagining Doobie’s as the home of a fictional couple whose possessions and memories have accumulated over generations. The result unfolds through a succession of intimate rooms: the Grand Salon, a velvet-lined rotunda, the Petit Salon, the Retour de Voyage, and an unexpected indoor garden beneath a glass roof. Mahogany, stained oak, dark marble, lacquered surfaces, and warm lighting establish an atmosphere that feels deliberately lived-in. Artworks, selected through visits to galleries and discoveries made during Behzadi’s travels, reinforce this impression. ‘I did it as a home, not as a restaurant,’ he explains, emphasizing that each object was chosen with the same instinct he would apply to his own living space.

Curiously, the project’s extended development became one of its greatest advantages. Structural complications delayed construction by several months, allowing Behzadi to revisit decisions and refine details that might otherwise have remained unresolved. The design now extends to the smallest architectural gestures, including the nocturnal bar with its lacquered mahogany and mirrored ceiling, and the downstairs washrooms, where artist Dominic J. Masullo has created a painted scene inspired by classical antiquity. For Behzadi, these interventions are meaningful only when they contribute to the larger narrative. ‘All the details have to have sense and meaning,’ he insists. He recalls overhearing two guests discussing the restaurant shortly after its reopening. Unaware that the architect was standing nearby, they remarked that whoever designed the place had clearly put his heart into it. It was, perhaps, a more meaningful compliment than any architectural review.

Some 460 kilometers southeast of Paris, Behzadi’s approach takes on an entirely different dimension at Pavyllon Lyon, the restaurant opened in September 2026 by Yannick Alléno and Institut Lyfe. Situated on Place Bellecour, the project is the world’s first Pavyllon restaurant-school, welcoming the public while providing approximately 600 students each year with practical experience alongside professional chefs and hospitality teams. Here, architecture must do considerably more than impress diners: it must also support an educational mission. ‘Hospitality is first an emotion, not beauty,’ Behzadi explains, recalling the moment he watched the students enter the completed restaurant for the first time. Their excitement moved him profoundly, confirming that the atmosphere he had sought to create was being experienced by the very people

This respect for authenticity becomes particularly important in a restaurant where the next generation of hospitality professionals is learning its craft. Rather than surrounding students with ostentatious luxury, Behzadi envisioned an environment that could communicate the values of French hospitality through proportion, materiality, and atmosphere. The dining room becomes a stage, with guests observing the movements of chefs and students, while the architecture quietly supports their interaction. ‘We were very aligned on not going too much into luxury. And if it’s luxury, it has to be very calm,’ he explains. The project’s success, in his view, has little to do with spectacular architectural gestures. What matters is the energy that emerges when people occupy the space, interact with one another, and feel comfortable enough to make it their own.

Beyond these two projects, Behzadi’s philosophy raises a broader question about the future of hospitality architecture. In an industry increasingly fascinated by visual novelty, he argues that restaurants and hotels should aspire to become enduring destinations rather than temporary spectacles. His ambition is to create places people will revisit in ten, fifteen, or twenty years and appreciate just as much as they did on their first visit. That sense of permanence also informs BAM, his furniture collection inspired by childhood memories of evenings spent on the rooftops of Tehran, where neighbors gathered beneath the stars to talk, share tea, and play backgammon.

Whether designing a chair or an entire restaurant, memory, human interaction, and emotional experience remain central to his thinking. ‘Design is a duty and a social responsibility,’ he concludes, insisting that the discipline must concern itself with far more than appearances. Ultimately, Doobie’s and Pavyllon Lyon illustrate the same conviction: the most memorable spaces are not necessarily those that demand to be looked at, but those that make us feel something worth remembering.

#9105. How to Calculate Your Rising and Moon Sign: A Beginner’s Guide

The sun sign is the *it girlie* of the “big three” elements in astrology.

But do you know about your moon sign and rising sign?

We chatted with an astrologer to understand what they are and how to calculate them.

According to Olga Verkhotina — astrologer and personal coach — the big three in astrology are your three most significant chart elements:

“While a natal chart contains so many more intricate details beyond just three elements, the big three is a way to determine the main highlights that make up your personality and overall temperament,” Verkhotina says.

Verkhotina explains that a rising sign is the zodiac sign that falls at the beginning of your First House — basically, the beginning of your natal chart.

“The First House in astrology is associated with a person’s identity, individual activity, even their appearance, and the sign that houses that theme gives its characteristics,” she says.

“Knowing your rising sign describes the way others may perceive you, the way your behavior comes across, as well as how you approach new situations in life.”

You’ll need: date, time and place of birth.

“Knowing the accurate time is important here because even 10 minutes can make a difference in the sign,” Verkhotina explains.

“Once you have the data, you can trust astrology software to calculate it for you. There are a lot of natal chart calculators online, so you can just search ‘rising sign calculator,'” Verkhotina says.

Pro tip: Verkhotina suggests reading horoscopes from your rising sign instead of your sun sign, saying it will likely give more personalized insights on which areas of your life might be impacted by current cosmic events.

“A moon sign describes the position of the moon on the zodiac wheel at the moment of your birth,” Verkhotina says.

She explains that the moon in astrology symbolizes:

“The moon sign helps you better understand how these themes demonstrate themselves in your life,” Verkhotina says.

Unlike the rising sign, you don’t have to have the precise time of birth to know your moon sign, although Verkhotina says it’s still recommended.

You can also use an online calculator to find your moon sign or refer to the ephemeris — a table showing the daily positions of planets.

Verkhotina describes the sun sign as the most important planet in your chart.

“It’s the center of your vitality, your ego, consciousness, and individuality at its core. That’s why it’s the most commonly known element in astrology,” she says.

It represents the zodiac sign the sun was in at the time of your birth, which Verkhotina says gives your individuality certain qualities associated with its specific sign.

“It’s important to understand that although the sun is a huge element in astrology, it doesn’t cover the nuances of one’s character,” Verkhotina explains.

Instead, she says it just represents overall traits.

Verkhotina adds that the specifics of your character are covered in the rest of your astrological chart. “This is why sometimes no two leos are the same,” she says.

This one is easy peasy — you don’t have to have your time or place of birth.

“The sun cycle is very similar every year, so you can look it up by the date, month and year of your birth. Each sign corresponds to a calendar date that year,” Verkhotina says.

Here’s each astro sign, in a nutshell, according to Verkhotina.

Your sun sign is important, but your moon and rising signs add extra details.

Your rising sign reflects your identity and how others see you, while your moon sign reveals your emotions and behavior.

To find these signs, you can use online birth chart calculators. Just make sure you have your birth date and time handy for accurate results.

#9104. Mori AI home robot "resembles a contemporary table lamp"

Robotics startup OKA has released a lamp-shaped artificial intelligence robot designed to offer companionship by greeting people, dancing to music and playing nature sounds.

Mori by OKA (One Kind Artificat) is 26.4 centimetres tall, with a cloth-covered base and an illuminated, dome-shaped head that lifts to reveal cartoonish eyes that blink and swivel.

According to OKA, Mori “resembles a contemporary table lamp” and was designed to “help people feel calmer, more at ease, and more connected to the world around them”.

“We wanted Mori to feel like a familiar object in the home rather than an unfamiliar machine,” OKA told Dezeen. “Many robots look technical, mechanical, or overly human, while a lamp is something people already live with comfortably.”

The robot exists in two modes: a lamp setting, when it’s compact and at rest, and a responsive setting, when the head is lifted and tilted.

Powered by the start-up’s proprietary AI system, the robot’s responses include playing audio informed by rain and other nature sounds, changing the colour of its lamp top and performing nonverbal communication through multi-axis neck and body movement.

Users tap the top of Mori’s head and it “retracts its face and becomes a quiet lamp”. As another part of its calming offerings, grabbing its base triggers a breathing exercise.

It also makes small sounds as part of these interactions.

“Mori’s soft silhouette and tactile materials let it blend into domestic interiors,” said OKA. “Its warmth, brightness, and subtle changes can suggest comfort, curiosity, or calm, which lets Mori express itself through illumination, sound, and movement instead of screens or conversation.”

According to the company, Mori will remember occupants, routines, and interaction history and adjust its behaviour accordingly, such as using “judgment to decide when to proactively engage or remain quiet”.

The AI model is based on the concept of Attentive Intelligence, built upon research by OKA co-founder Weizhe Chen. Attentive Intelligence is an emerging framework within AI, wherein a model is proactive versus reactive to prompts.

“It reads the room before responding and weighs whether to join in, so sometimes a small nod is enough and sometimes it stays quiet,” said OKA.

“Its responses are shaped by VIBE (Vitality, Interaction, Bonding, Emotion), an inner state that drifts with time and experience, so the same greeting can come out lively one day and gentle the next.”Mori comes in a variety of soft colourways and is rechargeable with a 2.5-hour battery life. However, OKA suggests keeping it plugged in.

OKA was founded in 2024 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, by entrepreneur and designer Hua Wang and robotics researcher Weizhe Che. The company is focused on creating robotic projects that “integrate seamlessly into human life rather than forcing human life to adapt to technology”.

OKA plans to release five major “artifacts” or products in its lifetime, according to the team. The Mori robot is the first.

Mori joins a growing number of home robots released recently with “embodied AI” – or the act of inserting an AI model into a robotic body.

Other home robots include the Droxel “droid butler” and Neo, a humanoid robot dressed in a cloth bodysuit.

#9102. Yoga and Overweight: Health Benefits and Tips for Getting Started

Part of the beauty of yoga is its accessibility for everyone. Yoga practitioners come in all shapes and sizes and are hella modifiable. If you have overweight, there’s 100% a place for you in the world of downward dogs, crescent lunges, and resting pigeons.

Check out these benefits of yoga for overweight.

For wellness, you’d be hard-pressed to find a more holistic practice than yoga. Your physical and mental health can get a boost from busting out your mat.

The limb-stretching, muscle-engaging, bodyweight-bearing nature of yoga has many physical benefits.

For starters, yoga may enhance your metabolism. An older study found that people who practiced had greater metabolic efficiency and lower weight than non-yogis.

It’s clear, too, that yoga’s combo of cardio and strength torches calories. A 160-pound person can burn around 180 calories per hour, popping in and out of poses. A 2021 study revealed that both Hatha and vinyasa yoga led to weight loss, with an average of 3.4 kilograms (7.5 pounds) lost over a 6-month.

Extra strength and flexibility are two other well-known upsides of the practice. Research shows that even sedentary folks can build these elements of fitness by taking up yoga. One study showed that, after 8 weeks of practicing at least twice a week (180 minutes), people with no prior yoga experience had greater muscle strength, endurance, flexibility, and cardio-respiratory fitness.

On the surface, yoga might look like mere stretching — but the practice goes far beyond the physical. Yoga engages the mind in all sorts of ways that may have benefits for overweight.

By training your brain toward calm and focus, yoga sessions encourage mindfulness. A mindful outlook can have far-reaching effects in multiple areas of life, like promoting mindful eating and greater body awareness.

As a form of self-care, yoga can also promote a healthier body image. In a 2018 study, young adults who made it a habit reported higher satisfaction levels with their bodies. Better self-esteem and motivation have also been linked to the practice.

Then, too, yoga’s stress-relieving effects might follow you off the mat and into the dining room. Some research has found that people who do yoga binge eat less often.

Wanna get started with yoga but aren’t sure how? We got you.

It all starts with setting realistic goals and expectations. If you’ve never practiced before, you won’t be pretzel-ing yourself into challenging poses like scorpion or crow overnight — and that’s OK. Consider setting smaller, step-wise goals, such as attending a 30-minute class twice a week or mastering a few basic poses. Little by little, you’ll work your way up to a more advanced practice.

It’s also wise to select a class (or video) for beginners. Check your gym or yoga studio’s schedule for introductory sessions, and don’t be afraid to let an instructor know before class that you may need some modifications. Most are happy to provide adaptations to make the class a better experience for beginners.

Meanwhile, if you’re pursuing a yoga practice for weight loss, remember to pair it with other healthy lifestyle practices for best results. Though stretching and holding poses burn calories, yoga might not take you to your weight loss goal alone. A balanced diet, cardio exercise, and sufficient sleep are other keys to achieving a healthy weight.

Yoga stereotypes of scantily clad gym babes in impossible contortions might make you feel somewhat intimidated about in-person classes. If you’re concerned that a gym session will make you self-conscious, start with an at-home practice. (YouTube is a treasure trove of classes and instructors explicitly geared for people with overweight.) All by yourself in your living room, there’s no one to impress.

Or, if you’re up for in-person yoga, let your instructor know your needs again. Modifications are always possible.

No matter where you practice, credit yourself for showing up for your health. And, at the beginning of your session, don’t forget to set an intention you find motivating or encouraging, such as “I am caring for my body” or “I am worthy of love and respect.”

Overweight doesn’t have to be a barrier to taking up yoga. Start small, knowing that you’ll get more comfortable with each session. With all the physical and mental health benefits a yoga practice provides — and all the modifications that make it more accessible — it’s worth a try, regardless of weight.

#9101. PPAA creates twin houses in Mexico as an "argument for building less"

Mexican architecture studio Pérez Palacios Arquitectos Asociados has completed twin houses that combine concrete with glued-laminated timber in the forests of Valle de Bravo, Mexico.

The two houses – each measuring 500 square metres (5,382 square feet) – are collectively called Rejas and were designed for two brothers and their families, cohabitating on a 1.2-acre forested property in Avándaro, a couple of hours west of Mexico City.

“Avándaro is a landscape that’s been quietly overbuilt for decades, so the first decision on Rejas was actually a renunciation,” Pablo Pérez Palacios, founder of Pérez Palacios Arquitectos Asociados (PPAA), told Dezeen,

“Instead of designing a wall or a fence between the two brothers’ houses, we chose to regenerate the native forest that the site had partially lost, and let that stand as the boundary,” he said, explainging that decision set the tone for the rest of the project.

“The whole project is really an argument for building less, so the landscape has room to eventually reclaim the architecture.”

The site, with its regenerated forest, is steeply sloped toward the Avándaro reservoir, allowing PPAA to partially submerge each house.

From the driveway, the houses appear as one-storey structures, but the lower levels emerge on the other side as the terrain descends.

To navigate this, the houses sit on bases of concrete and local stone that anchor them into the slope, while timber roofs top the upper levels and open the spaces to the surrounding trees.

The houses were designed to interact with the landscape, and have almost identical plans, though their place in the landscape differs.

Public spaces are on the upper level, with a kitchen, dining and living room in a glass box within the larger, rectangular platform.

A covered terrace comprises the remainder of the level with designated seating and outdoor cooking areas that are framed with planters.

Below, five bedrooms with ensuite bathrooms and a lounge area sit within the forest floor, cool and contained within the boxy volume.

“The deliberate positioning of the openings eliminates any possibility of facing windows – no window in one house looks toward the other. Each dwelling establishes its own relationship with the natural surroundings as if the other did not exist.”

The studio pulled the service areas for both houses into separate buildings placed along the edge of the property to free the centre of the plot for the houses and their relationships with the landscape.

Designed to patina with the landscape, the minimalist material palette relies on stone and concrete to give mass and solidity to the base and mass timber to be both the structure and spatial character of the upper level.

The pairing allows the materials to complement one another, juxtaposing lightness and weight.

“This tension between the stone base that anchors and the glulam roof that liberates is neither an aesthetic operation nor a reference to any vernacular tradition,” the studio said.

“It is a proposition about how to inhabit: what protects and what opens, what remains and what breathes, what belongs to the ground and what belongs to the air.”

Long known for concrete construction like this subtractive house in Los Angeles, PPAA has been expanding recently into mass timber design with projects like a rotating cross-laminated timber pavilion in Mexico City and Mexico’s first “all-wood” mass timber structure in Querétaro.

#9100. Having ‘Boring’ Conversations Is Really Good for You, Psychologists Say

It’s tempting to try to bypass coworkers in the break room or limit small talk with the person waiting next to you in an effort to avoid what you suspect will be a dull conversation. But new research makes a solid argument for leaning into these “boring” chats.

The study, which was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that people who actually engage in these conversations thought that they were much more interesting and enjoyable than they expected. But beyond that, there is data to suggest that having these “boring” conversations could do your mental and physical health a solid.

“These moments are small, but they are not trivial,” Nicholas Allan, PhD, psychologist and assistant professor in the department of psychiatry and behavioral health at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. Here’s why.

The research focused on nine experiments featuring 1,800 participants. During the experiments, participants were asked to predict how much they would enjoy talking about a range of topics they identified as boring. These included World Wars I and II, nonfiction books, math, onions, the stock market, cats, and vegan diets. These chats happened with either strangers or friends, and were in person or online.

The researchers discovered that while participants said they expected the conversations to be pretty lame, they reported afterward that they enjoyed them much more than they thought they would. This even happened when both people in the conversation thought a topic was boring.

“We decided to conduct this research because so many people avoid conversations they think will be boring. We cancel small talk, dread networking events, and assume that certain topics, like the weather, commuting, or daily routines, just won’t be interesting,” Elizabeth Trinh, lead study author and a doctoral student at the University of Michigan, tells SELF. “If conversations are generally good for us, why do we so often expect them to be dull or draining?”

Ultimately, the researchers found that being engaged in the conversation was what really mattered. “Engagement drives enjoyment more than topic does,” Trinh says. “People assume that interest comes from having a fascinating subject. But in reality, what makes conversations enjoyable is the sense of connection like feeling heard, responding to each other, and discovering unexpected details about someone’s life. Even a mundane topic can become meaningful when two people are actively engaging with each other.”

People are social creatures by nature and connecting over a topic that feels boring, like onions, is still a social connection, Aaron P. Brinen, PsyD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, tells SELF. Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor of psychology at NYU Langone Health, agrees. “Sometimes people will predict that a conversation will be awkward or uncomfortable. But if you try to connect and listen in a conversation, there can be great benefits,” she tells SELF.

As a result, Dr. Gallagher says she encourages her patients to have conversations everywhere they go. “Being a lifelong learner can be very powerful,” she says. “At the end of the day, connecting with humans can make us feel good.”

These chats can seem pointless, but experts stress that they’re actually not. Not only will you likely find that you enjoy “boring” conversations more than you expected, it could keep you from feeling lonely.

“Loneliness is not just about how many people someone sees. It is about whether interactions feel connecting and meaningful,” explains Dr. Allan. Side-stepping a “boring” chat is likely to increase your sense of loneliness, Dr. Brinen says. “Even if you didn’t want to be a part of that conversation, you’re still lonely,” he points out.

Loneliness on its own is a horrible feeling, but it can also have a big impact on your health. Feeling lonely or socially isolated raises the risk of a slew of serious health conditions, including heart disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, depression, anxiety, dementia, and early death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). “When we find a way to be engaged with other people, it meets that need to connect with others,” Dr. Brinen says.

Over time, those small “boring” moments can build on each other, Dr. Allan says. With that, your feelings of loneliness—and health risks that can come with them—decrease.

Of course, some interactions with others aren’t great. “Not all social contact is beneficial,” Dr. Allan says. “More contact is not automatically better. What seems to matter most is whether the interaction feels respectful, reciprocal, and emotionally safe. Positive connection helps. Depleting or hostile interactions do not.”

Ultimately, Trinh recommends keeping an open mind when it comes to future conversations. “We may be missing out on connection because we misjudge how conversations will feel,” she says. “If we avoid talking to someone because we assume it will be boring—like a coworker at the coffee machine, a stranger at an event, or a neighbor in the elevator—we may be unnecessarily depriving ourselves of small moments of connection that could improve our mood and sense of belonging.”

#9099. Shaw Contract Design Awards name top interiors of 2026

A Japanese office intended to evoke a tree canopy, and a revived US concert hall are among the interior design projects to win Best of Globe at this year’s Shaw Contract Design Awards.

The upgrade of an athletics clubhouse in the US, a legal workplace in the UK and a large three-story office in India also took the top prize in the annual award programme, now in its 21st year.

Held annually by flooring manufacturer Shaw Contract, the Shaw Contract Design Awards celebrate interior design projects that “spark creativity, connect communities and contribute to a better, more sustainable world”.

This year’s winning projects were selected from nearly 550 global submissions by an international jury of architects and designers, with interior design students also joining as part of Shaw’s commitment to supporting the next generation of design talent.

According to the jury, the 2026 winners were unified by “a clear design narrative, an understanding of local context, varied and inclusive user experiences, responsible material strategies and a meaningful relationship between design intent and completed space” – despite their varying scales and styles.

“Throughout the global judging session, the jury returned to a central question: whether each project’s stated intent was visible and understandable in the completed design,” explained Shaw Contract.

“The panel distinguished between attractive spaces and projects that used planning, materials, detail and experience to communicate a clear and consequential idea.”

The St Louis Symphony Orchestra Powell Hall in the US, overhauled by Christner Architects, was one of the winners.

According to Shaw Contract, the jury selected it for its sensitive balance of old and new elements, as well as the important social role it plays in the city, thanks to improved accessibility and audience facilities.

Also in the US is the winning Missouri Athletic Club project, completed by HOK. The scheme involved revamping an existing clubhouse to better suit the needs of its current members.

HOK’s design was commended for adding “a new layer to the club’s heritage rather than treating the past as a fixed visual theme”, according to the brand, introducing a contemporary layout and aesthetic.

The third winner was We Labo 25F, a small workspace in Japan that embodies the principles of biophilic design – the use of natural features such as plants to improve the wellbeing of building occupants.

Its architect, Okamura, was praised for incorporating greenery as more than just “a decorative layer” and creating an interior that mimics working beneath a tree canopy.

The office was also selected in recognition of its adaptable interiors and circular design features, including furniture made from tsunami debris.

We Labo 25F was one of three workplaces to win Best of Globe, alongside Diageo by M Moser Associates in India and DLA Piper by Sheppard Robson Architects in the UK.

Diageo spans 7,700 square metres and accommodates 300 employees across each of its three floors, accommodating its owner’s expansion from Bengaluru to Gurugram.

It was selected by the jury for its “richly layered and carefully crafted” interiors, which combine a wide range of workspaces with shared hospitality areas. M Moser Associates dedicated more than half of the building to community spaces.

Finally, DLA Piper by Sheppard Robson Architects is a large workplace for a legal company. It was designed to cater to different work styles.

According to Shaw Contract, it won the prize for providing a broad range of workspaces suited to different needs, as well as wellbeing, dining and meeting areas.

The jury particularly enjoyed how materials had been applied in a way that adds “warmth and richness into areas that might traditionally be treated as purely corporate”.

The Best of Globe winners are selected from the programme’s Best of Region winners. Winners receive global media exposure and a donation to a charity of their choice.

Shaw Contract’s ambition for the award programme is to encourage discourse within the international creative community.

#9098. Starvation Mode: How Caloric Restriction Affects Your Body

Cutting back on calories but not losing weight? You might wonder if you’ve gotten stuck in the twilight zone of so-called “starvation mode.”

Everyone from your personal trainer to your grandma may have warned you about this metabolic frenemy that keeps your body holding onto weight. But is starvation mode really a thing — or just an urban legend?

The concept of starvation mode is that when you restrict calories, your body has a “hold it right there” response. To prevent you from losing weight rapidly, your metabolism slows, conserving energy by reducing the calories it burns.

Research shows starvation mode — formally called adaptive thermogenesis or metabolic adaptation — is a legit phenomenon. It’s well documented that sometimes, the more weight you lose (and the more rapidly you do so), the more your body resists the process.

Evolutionarily speaking, this may be a holdover from when humans faced food scarcity and needed a mechanism for self-preservation. But in today’s world, starvation mode can be a frustrating roadblock to weight loss.

What does this metabolic hiccup look like? These symptoms may indicate that starvation mode is becoming a problem for your health:

Starvation mode isn’t the same thing as actual starving. In today’s modern food environment, true starvation is rare. If you’re eating regularly, you won’t experience life-threatening starvation.

However, your body might exhibit some of the same early signs as real starvation. These include the symptoms listed above.

Most commonly, though, starvation mode involves stalled weight loss. You may have hit the wall of adaptive thermogenesis when restricting calories and increasing physical activity without losing weight.

Getting into starvation mode can take just a few days, especially if those days involve severe calorie restriction.

So what counts as severe calorie restriction? Many experts advise not going below 1,200 calories per day for women and 1,500 calories per day for men unless supervised by a doctor. Anything below these numbers could land you in starvation mode faster.

Fortunately, getting your body out of starvation mode isn’t complicated.

First, there’s the obvious solution: Eat a few more calories. But we don’t mean just any calories. By adding a few more nutrient-dense foods (especially those with fiber and protein), you may find weight loss becomes easier, not harder. Both of these nutrients have links to weight loss — so they might help you get out of starvation mode without gaining weight.

If you’re feeling extremely depleted, you might take a temporary break from a weight loss diet to replenish your nutrient stores.

Choosing the proper exercise could also bump you out of starvation mode. Resistance exercises like weightlifting, yoga, push-ups, squats, and others build muscle, which increases your metabolic rate.

According to a 2014 study, people who participated in a 9-month resistance exercise program increased their resting metabolic rate — aka how many calories they burned at rest — by an average of 5%.

Weight loss is a balancing act. It’s normal to experience physical and emotional ups and downs.

That said, it’s time to see a doctor if you’re noticing symptoms like extreme fatigue or lethargy, constipation that lasts more than a few days, sensitivity to cold, or unusual mood changes. Your healthcare team can help you hit the sweet spot of weight loss without lingering in starvation mode.

Despite its name, being in starvation mode doesn’t mean you’ll starve. Instead, it’s a state in which your body has adapted to your weight loss efforts, giving you pushback on how many calories it burns. With strategies like tweaking your calorie intake and adding strength training, you can get out of this mode and back on the path to sustained weight loss.

Last medically reviewed on August 31, 2024

#9097. Incline Walking vs. Running: What’s the Better Workout?

Incline walking and running are commonly framed as opposites: one is low impact, the other is high-intensity. But in reality, they’re both effective cardio options that challenge your body in distinct ways—from the muscles you recruit to the impact on your joints. Both workouts can boost your heart health, build endurance, and leave you seriously sweaty, but they place different demands on your body, according to Gab Reznik, CPT and Tone House coach. The question isn’t which is better across the board—it’s which is better for you depending on your goals.

Understanding those differences can help you decide which one deserves a spot in your fitness routine, or how to incorporate both.

At their core, incline walking and running share a common foundation: they get your body moving in a rhythmic, repetitive way that challenges your cardiovascular system.

“Any movement is better than no movement at all—whether that’s incline walking or running,” Reznik tells SELF. “They’re both effective at increasing blood flow, elevating heart rate, and improving overall aerobic capacity.” That means stronger heart and lung function over time—which are key markers of long-term health.

They also both demand muscular effort. Running requires you to generate power with every stride, while incline walking emphasizes controlled, deliberate steps against gravity (thanks to the incline). “Over time, the repetitive impact and loading can help strengthen joints and support long-term durability when done properly,” Reznik says.

While they may look similar on the surface, incline walking and running are different in two major ways: how hard they push your body, and how much stress they place on your joints.

Running is the higher-impact option. With each stride, your joints absorb roughly two to three times your body weight. That added force typically translates to higher intensity—and more calories burned per hour, Reznik explains.

Incline walking, on the other hand, keeps one foot on the ground at all times, reducing overall joint load. “Incline walking is more sustainable for longer durations,” Reznik says. “At the same fitness level, someone will typically be able to maintain an incline walk longer than a run due to the lower per-step demand.”

It’s easy to think of incline walking as purely cardio—but that’s only part of its benefits.

“Incline walking can absolutely build strength, just not in the same way as lifting weights,” Reznik says. Instead of maximizing muscle growth by picking up heavy weights, incline walking improves muscular endurance, particularly in the lower body (think: glutes, hamstrings, and calves).

The steeper the incline, the greater the challenge. And if you want to level up even more, try adding external load, like a weighted vest, Reznik suggests. “It can increase the strength stimulus without significantly increasing joint impact.”

Still, it’s important to keep your expectations realistic. If your goal is to build maximal strength or increase muscle size, traditional strength training should still be your primary focus.

One of the biggest misconceptions about incline walking is that it’s somehow inferior to running. Reznik is quick to shut that down.

“Walking isn’t less effective—it’s simply a different type of stimulus,” she says.

In fact, incline walking can be deceptively tough. Imagine this: a 15% incline at 3 mph for 30 minutes, without holding onto the treadmill. “That’s extremely challenging—even for a trained runner,” Reznik says.

Both workouts can improve cardiovascular fitness and support fat loss when programmed appropriately. The key is understanding that “effective” doesn’t mean “hardest”—it means the movement is aligned with your fitness goals.

If you’re aiming to maximize calorie burn in a shorter amount of time or really test your cardiovascular endurance, running may be the more efficient choice, Reznik says. Its higher intensity makes it ideal for pushing your limits.

But if you’re looking to reduce joint stress while still building aerobic fitness (and even some muscular endurance), incline walking may be the smarter pick. “If you treat them as complementary, you can unlock a higher level of performance and longevity,” Reznik says.

Deciding between incline walking and running ultimately comes down to three factors: your goals, your current fitness level, and what you actually enjoy enough to stick with.

Beginners might start with a light jog at a conversational pace or a slight incline (around 2% to 3%) at a comfortable walking speed, Reznik suggests. From there, it’s important to progress either the speed or incline, but not both at once.

“Incline walking isn’t the ‘easy’ option—it’s the smart option when used correctly,” Reznik says. “Running isn’t the ‘better’ option—it’s the specific option when it aligns with your goals.”

A well-rounded routine might include both: running for higher-intensity days when you want to challenge your cardio limits, and incline walking for longer, lower-impact sessions that still deliver a serious burn.

Ultimately, there’s no clear winner between incline walking and running because they aren’t rivals. Both movements can be tools for improving heart health, building endurance and strengthening key muscle groups. The better workout is the one that helps you move consistently and safely. And in many cases, the smartest approach isn’t choosing between them—it’s using both.

#9096. Caá Porá Arquitectura and Jerome Haferd Studio design drum-like performance centre for Ecuador

Ecuadorian studio Caá Porá Arquitectura has teamed up with US-based Jerome Haferd Studio and engineer Juan Sebastián Pérez for the Bombódromo performance centre in Carchi, Ecuador.

The building will feature a central venue that has massive bamboo support elements based on local drums.

The campus will include dozens of buildings centred around a massive auditorium in the province of Carchi, north of Quito, sited along the Chota River in an Andean valley.

Masterplanned by Caá Porá Arquitectura, the campus was designed for local government to celebrate Afro-Ecuadorian culture.

Based on this, the central performance centre has a design based on the bomba, a drum used by local people.

“The inspiration for a lot of the design language was kind of to bridge African and Andean kind of design languages and ancestral aesthetics,” Jerome Haferd told Dezeen.

“That is embodied in the bomba drum, which is a unique instrument that is made by the people in this region, who we worked with very closely to come up with the design concept for the master plan.”

“[The bomba] was adapted and generated out of materials local to this valley in Ecuador, and so it’s really a hybrid between the Andean mountains and Africa.”

The main performance space, designed to hold more than 10,000, will have massive bundles of laminated bamboo supporting a roof system 30 metres in diameter.

These bundled columns have been designed to feature laminated bamboo and timber elements, reflecting the construction of the bomba drum and local construction methods more generally.

Acoustic fabric will hang from the wooden rafters of the semi-enclosed performance space.

A series of stone buildings will flank the main performance space, forming the back-of-house facilities.

An outdoor area will feature a tiered gathering space tucked into the low-lying trees around the river and provide the main viewing platforms for the performances.

As many as eight outbuildings will feature on the campus, including classrooms, a restaurant and artisan kiosks.

These structures will be built with metal roofs and rammed-earth walls, furthering the connection to local building techniques.

“The result is a radical, place-based reinterpretation of how a performing arts venue can respond to a unique cultural context while accommodating flexible uses,” said the team, which worked with local group Fundación Casa Oshun for the community outreach.

The project is expected to break ground in 2027.

Recently, a team including SANAA, Caá Porá Arquitectura, Estudio A0 and Jerome Haferd Studio was selected to design the National Museum of Ecuador in Quito, after the original design was cancelled following community backlash.

#9095. Text Neck Exercises: Simple Moves to Ease Digital Strain

Whether you’re caught up in doomscrolling or just checking your work emails, chances are you’re spending a lot of time on your phone. But all that screen time can lead to a pesky condition called “text neck.” Hunching over your device can leave you with some severe aches and pains.

So, hold your phone up to eye level and check out these easy tips to get rid of text neck fast!

Also known as “tech neck,” text neck is a term coined by a chiropractor to describe the neck pain you might feel after spending too much time looking down at your phone.

Most of us check our phones with our heads tilted forward and down. When you do this for too long, the muscles in your neck get strained. The muscles in the back are overstretched, while the ones in the front are compressed.

If you have text neck, here’s what you might be dealing with:

But don’t get bent out of shape about overusing your favorite device. There’s no solid proof that your phone habits are to blame for your neck woes. Several studies found no connection between using your device and having neck or shoulder pain.

You could get a sore neck from overusing your muscles for many other reasons, like genetic factors, weight issues, or bad posture. “Text neck” might be a term concocted by a chiropractor to get your business. But, hey, we’re not judging.

To help ease text neck pain, try these simple exercises.

Aside from these cubicle-friendly exercises, here are some ideas to help keep text neck from being a regular pain in the y’know:

“Text neck” is the popular term for the head and neck pain caused by hunching over your device for too long. But don’t throw away your beloved device just yet. More research is needed to link “text neck” to your tech time.

In the meantime, sit up straight and do gentle exercises like neck rolls, chin tucks, and shoulder rolls. To prevent text neck from hitting you up on the reg, take regular breaks from your phone and seek out habits that help lengthen and strengthen your body. Your neck will thank you!

#9094. How to Have Great Sex After 60, According to Experts

There’s a common assumption that great, adventurous sex is a young person’s game—and with age, it fades into something boring, nonexistent, or just…not worth the effort.

Growing up, Karen Bigman fell for the propaganda. “But recently, I’ve done it in restaurant bathrooms,” Bigman, a 62-year-old certified sex educator, tells SELF, before listing off other examples of her scandalous escapades. “I’ve spontaneously met up in hotel rooms when the kids were at home. We even pulled over next to a Duane Reade [convenience store], under the fluorescent lamp, to do it in the back seat of his car.”

To be clear, sex isn’t always this spontaneous for Bigman. But in both her own life and her work with clients, she insists sex in this stage of life isn’t just happening: It’s getting better. For some, it’s even kinkier—though it’s a reality you rarely hear about and probably don’t want to imagine your parents or grandparents doing.

The fear that your sex life dies with age doesn’t come from nowhere. Bodies change. Menopause (which typically starts in a person’s 40s or 50s) can bring on a slew of symptoms like vaginal dryness or painful sex. Hormonal shifts can lower libido across all sexes. Energy levels fluctuate—and acting out on desires that once felt automatic may now require more effort, communication, and patience.

Still, none of this has to spell the end of a satisfying bedroom life, according to both sex therapists and real people enjoying sex after 60. Here’s how they maintain the spark—and the small shifts they say make the biggest differences.

Vaginal dryness is one of the most common physical changes that comes with aging—and it’s why many people assume getting frisky in this stage will be uncomfortable or painful.

However, there are plenty of expert-recommended products designed to help, and lube is one of the most effective and underrated. “Put it on before you start and have it at the ready during sex,” Bigman, who also shares her advice on her Taboo to Truth: Life & Sex After 50 podcast, says. Lubricants work by reducing friction, which means less risk of irritation or tearing—and just as importantly, more room for pleasure. For best results, we also recommend applying it not just to the penetrating object (like a penis or vibrator) and what’s being penetrated (your vagina), but also during foreplay—for example, consider sliding between labial folds too. (If you’re unsure what lube to buy, start with this beginner-friendly article.)

In some situations, the issue may not be physical or logistical. It’s that the sex you’re having just…isn’t that great.

“If you’re in a relationship or marriage where sex is not exciting, of course you’re not going to want to do it,” Tammy Nelson, PhD, a 63-year-old AASECT-certified sex therapist, who also speaks from personal experience, tells SELF. “It’s like, if the party isn’t fun, why would you go?”

However, one of the many upsides of getting older is acquiring a kind of bluntness your younger self probably shied away from. “At a certain point, you just don’t give a crap,” one 64-year-old woman, speaking anonymously, tells SELF. When you realize life’s too short, you stop worrying so much about how your body looks in certain lighting, how you sound while climaxing, and whether your kinks are “too much.”

“I was once so ashamed to bring up BDSM—being spanked, choked. You don’t want to scare someone off or be judged,” she says. But after years of what she calls “vanilla sex,” she discovered a game-changing truth: speaking up is worth it. “I had my first real orgasm—that I didn’t have to fake—at 61.”

Achieving a mind-blowing climax doesn’t require a partner. For the women SELF spoke with, their 50s and 60s marked a turning point in figuring out what made them squirm—where they enjoyed being touched, what kind of stimulation worked, which fantasies excited them—all thanks to masturbation.

“I feel freer now to explore my body,” Shay Martin, 63, who owns Vibratex (the exclusive distributor of the Magic Wand sex toy brand), tells SELF. “When I was younger, I would use my hands manually, but there are so many tools out there [vibrators, anal toys, penis rings, nipple clamps] to help with achieving an orgasm on your own that’s much more intense and lasts longer.”

Research backs up the benefits of solo play: Not only does masturbation feel great, but it can also boost confidence in your sexuality (something older women are rarely encouraged to embrace) and relieve menopause-related symptoms like vaginal dryness, low sex drive, and mood changes. Once you figure out what feels good, “it becomes a whole lot easier to communicate exactly what you want from another person,” Dr. Nelson says—which makes settling for mediocre hookups (the kind you may have tolerated in your 20s) far less likely.

Bodies in their 60s don’t always cooperate the way they used to—and that’s okay.

An aching back and weak knees have made certain positions uncomfortable for Isma, 68. “Standard missionary can be tough, so I usually lie on my side with my husband spooning behind me,” she tells SELF. (Another option experts previously recommended to SELF includes child’s pose, which can give you better control over the positioning of your back. Or, for pelvic pain, you can hop on top to adjust the depth of penetration and keep it shallow.)

Sometimes, Isma says she uses a wedged, foam pillow under her hips for extra support too. (Yes, there are specialized sex pillows that stay sturdy and don’t flatten out, helping you maintain the right angle without discomfort.) “It’s not as effortless or spontaneous as it used to be,” Isma admits, reflecting on how creating intimacy has changed throughout the years. “But we’ve learned our ways to make it work.”

According to Dr. Nelson, it’s a common misconception that sex is only “good” when it includes penetration and ends in an orgasm. But expanding your definition—not by lowering your standards but by adjusting them—can keep intimacy exciting and realistic.

That might mean focusing on in-the-moment sensations over outcomes: slower pacing, more touch, less pressure to cum. “He genuinely loves going down on me,” Isma says of her husband, describing a nightly, pre-bed ritual that they have maintained almost every day for the past five years. “I don’t usually finish, and neither does he. It just feels amazing. We always look forward to it.”

Martin has found something similar through practicing erotic massages. “At first I was intimidated, because you hear so much about the decline in libido, pain, lack of newness.” Now, Martin says, the slow buildup and warm oil rubbing throughout her erogenous zones is what she anticipates most.

While sex after 60 may not be the kind of stuff that makes it onto racy TV scenes (for now!), that’s precisely what experts say gives it power: It’s a slow, personalized intimacy built only through decades of experimentation, exploration, and curiosity—the kind that only gets better with age.

#9093. Sumayya Vally to design Dubai art foundation around the "memory of a house"

South African architect Sumayya Vally is designing a permanent home for the Elie Khouri Art Foundation (EKAF), which will be located within a renovated villa in Dubai.

Set to be built in the Jumeirah 1 development in Dubai, the foundation’s home will be located in a former villa, which will be dramatically overhauled by Vally – principal of architecture studio Counterspace.

“I think of buildings as having many lives,” said Vally. “At EKAF, we begin with a house that has already held a world within it. Its doors, cornices, balustrades, and particular ways of receiving people and separating rooms contain the traces of another life,” she continued.

“I am interested in what happens when we take these intimate geometries and give them a new public scale: when the architecture of a room becomes the architecture of a city-facing facade, and the memory of a house becomes the beginnings of an institution.”

Although few details of the design have been revealed, a render shows what appears to be a three-storey building with a light pink textured facade.

Lines across the facade appear to suggest fragments of the previous building, with recognisable shapes including doorways visible. Geometric holes punched in the facade will reveal activities taking place inside.

EKAF was established by Lebanese-French businessman Elie Khouri and its permanent home is planned to open in 2028. The foundation will contain gallery space to show its permanent collection and will also include space for temporary exhibits.

“I hope that artists, designers, researchers and makers from the region will bring other imaginations into the work, and that the institution will continue to acquire forms and meanings we cannot yet anticipate,” added Vally.

Designer of the Serpentine Pavilion in 2021, Vally was named emerging architect of the year at Dezeen Awards in 2023 and one of Time magazine’s 100 leaders of the future in 2021.

Earn Alaska miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa, Marriott Bonvoy transfers (3:1 ratio with 5K bonus per 60K), or direct purchase during sales. Target 60,000 miles for a one-way business class ticket.

Use JAL's own award search tool to check business class availability before contacting Alaska. Search 331 days out from your desired travel date. Look for flights showing "Partner Award" availability on JAL's calendar.

Verify your target flight operates a Boeing 787 or 777 with JAL's "Sky Suite" business class product. Older aircraft on some routes may have a less desirable cabin configuration. Check SeatGuru or JAL's fleet page.

Phone Alaska's award desk at 1-800-252-7522. Have your dates, route, and JAL flight number ready. The agent will search their system and process the redemption. Expect $25-$50 in taxes and fees.

Log into JAL.com with your confirmation number to select your specific seat and pre-order your meal. JAL offers both Western and Japanese cuisine options in business class, and the Japanese multi-course kaiseki meal is the experience worth choosing.

A sweet spot that punches far above its weight in cents-per-mile value

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you see it, and understanding it will help you recognize similar opportunities across the loyalty landscape.

Most major airline programs have shifted to dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate with demand, just like cash prices. Alaska Mileage Plan has largely resisted this for its partner awards. JAL Business Class from North America is priced at a flat 60,000 Alaska miles one way, period. It doesn't matter if it's Golden Week in Japan or a random Tuesday in February. The chart price holds.

This creates an extraordinary opportunity because JAL cash fares are not fixed. They respond to demand, fuel costs, seasonality, and competitive dynamics. When those fares rise — as they have substantially in recent years — your 60,000 miles buy proportionally more value. The inefficiency widens the more expensive the cash fare becomes.

Here's a detail that separates Alaska from many other programs: Alaska Mileage Plan charges zero fuel surcharges on any partner award booking. This is significant. Some programs (looking at you, British Airways Avios) pass through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $400–$800 to a theoretically cheap award. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket is taxes only — typically $50–$150 on a transpacific itinerary. Your 60,000-mile redemption costs you 60,000 miles plus roughly $100. Full stop.

The Transfer Path: Marriott Bonvoy Is Your On-Ramp

Alaska Mileage Plan has no direct credit card transfer partners in the traditional Chase/Amex/Citi sense. This is the most important nuance of this redemption to understand. You cannot transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards directly to Alaska. Instead, the primary transfer path runs through Marriott Bonvoy.

The ratio is 3 Marriott points to 1 Alaska mile, and transfers typically take 1 to 5 days to complete. There's also the well-known Marriott bonus: transfer 60,000 Marriott points and receive 5,000 bonus miles, meaning 60,000 Marriott points nets you 25,000 Alaska miles. This makes earning Alaska miles via Marriott cards (like the Marriott Bonvoy Boundless or Brilliant) a viable — if not the most efficient — path.

The more efficient earning strategy for most ChooseFI members is to apply directly for the Alaska Airlines Visa card, which regularly offers strong welcome bonuses, or to fly Alaska-operated flights. Miles in Alaska Mileage Plan never expire, which means you can accumulate patiently without pressure.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — a benefit almost no other major US program offers anymore. On a one-way award from the US to Japan, you could stop in Tokyo for several days, then continue to another destination, all for the same 60,000 miles. This is an advanced move that can double the value of a single award ticket.

Book at up to 331 days in advance — Alaska's booking window. For popular travel dates to Japan, searching early is strongly advised.

Before you transfer a single point, confirm the seats exist. Go to jal.com and use JAL's own award search tool. JAL releases excellent Business Class award inventory to partners — this is one of the best-availability premium cabin routes in the game — but you still want to verify before committing.

Search your target dates in "Award Booking" mode. Look for "J" class availability (Business Class). JAL's 787-9 Sky Suite III product operates on the Seattle–Tokyo Narita route, so filter for that routing specifically. Try flexible dates — a day or two of flexibility can reveal significantly more availability. You can search up to 330+ days out, so don't wait until the last minute.

You need 60,000 Alaska Mileage Plan miles per one-way Business Class ticket. Check your existing Alaska Mileage Plan balance at alaskaair.com. If you're short, your transfer path is Marriott Bonvoy at a 3:1 ratio — so 60,000 Alaska miles requires 180,000 Marriott Bonvoy points (though you'll receive a 5,000-mile bonus when transferring 60,000 Marriott points at a time, so plan accordingly).

Initiate transfers at marriott.com under "Transfer Points." Build in 1 to 5 days for the transfer to post to your Alaska account. Do not call Alaska to book until the miles are confirmed in your balance.

Alaska partner awards with JAL must be booked by phone — you cannot book JAL awards on Alaska's website. Call Alaska Mileage Plan at 1-800-252-7522. Have the following ready:

Tell the agent you'd like to book a partner award on JAL using miles. Give them the exact flight number and date. Agents are generally familiar with this redemption — it's a popular one.

Before you finalize, confirm the total cost. Alaska charges no fuel surcharges on partner awards, so your out-of-pocket should be taxes only. If an agent quotes you a surcharge, politely clarify — this is a known Alaska policy. The total cash component should be well under $200.

If your ideal dates show no availability, try these tactics: search plus or minus three days, look at alternate departure cities (JAL also operates from Los Angeles, Chicago, and New York), or set a calendar reminder to check again — JAL sometimes releases additional inventory closer to departure as business travelers book and cancel. The 331-day booking window means early searchers have the best selection.

Alaska Airlines is not part of any major airline alliance (Star Alliance, Oneworld, or SkyTeam), which gives it unusual freedom to set its own partner award pricing. While alliance members must coordinate pricing frameworks, Alaska negotiates individual deals with each partner airline. This independence is why Alaska can price JAL business class at 60,000 miles when alliance-member programs charge 70,000-100,000 miles for the same seats. The tradeoff is that Alaska's partner award availability can be more limited than what you would find through an alliance booking, making timing and flexibility critical.

The Cash Price: Pull up JAL.com during late March and you'll routinely see Business Class fares at $7,000–$8,500 per person one way. For a couple, that's $14,000–$17,000 in cash for two seats in the premium cabin. Most people stare at that number and close the browser.

The Points Price: 60,000 Alaska miles per person. For two passengers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles plus approximately $200–$250 in taxes. Total cash outlay: roughly $225 for the pair.

The CPP: At a conservative $7,000 cash fare, 60,000 miles delivers 11.7 cents per point — nearly six times the standard benchmark for a great redemption.

For a couple targeting FI, spending 120,000 Alaska miles — earned largely through welcome bonuses and everyday spending — instead of $15,000+ in cash is the entire philosophy in action.

Alaska allows a free stopover on one-way awards — one of the most underused benefits in the program. Marriott-to-Alaska transfers take 1 to 5 days and are irreversible. Never initiate the transfer until you've confirmed the award space exists on JAL.com. Transferring speculatively and then discovering the seat is gone is a painful and costly mistake.

While JAL does release excellent inventory — hence the availability score of 4 out of 5 — "year round" availability doesn't mean unlimited. Japanese holidays (Golden Week, Obon in August, New Year's) see compressed availability. The best open inventory is typically September through November and January through mid-February.

Alaska's policy is no fuel surcharges on partner awards, but always verify the final tax-and-fee total before giving your credit card number. Your total out-of-pocket should be well under $200 per ticket. If it's higher, ask the agent to itemize.

This redemption is built for the ChooseFI couple or solo traveler who has been intentionally accumulating Alaska miles — or Marriott Bonvoy points — and wants to experience transpacific Business Class without the $8,000 price tag. Alaska has **no direct credit card transfer partners** in the major bank ecosystems, which means you can't funnel everyday Amex or Chase spend into Alaska miles directly. You're relying on Alaska co-branded credit cards or the Marriott Bonvoy transfer path. Second, partner award bookings **cannot be completed online** — you must call Alaska Mileage Plan. For travelers accustomed to booking everything digitally, this feels like friction. In practice, the call takes 15–20 minutes with a prepared agent and is genuinely straightforward. Third, while availability is rated 4 out of 5 (excellent by transpacific standards), you still need to plan ahead, particularly for peak Japan travel seasons. **Three tips to make it easier:** 1. **Start with the Alaska Airlines Visa card** — it's the most direct route to a large Alaska miles balance and regularly offers competitive welcome bonuses. 2. **Do your availability research on JAL.com before calling** — walk into that phone call with the flight number, date, and cabin class already confirmed. The best availability appears right at the 331-day booking window. Shoulder seasons like January-February and September-November tend to have more open seats. Cherry blossom season (late March through early April) and summer are the most competitive periods.

Marriott Bonvoy points transfer to Alaska at a 3:1 ratio. For every 60,000 Bonvoy points transferred, you receive 20,000 Alaska miles plus a 5,000-mile bonus, totaling 25,000 Alaska miles. To reach 60,000 Alaska miles, you would need approximately 135,000 Bonvoy points (factoring in the bonus on each 60K tranche).

Alaska Mileage Plan to JAL business class is one of the best-kept sweet spots in travel rewards. At 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges, you get access to a world-class cabin at roughly half the mileage cost of competing programs. The earning path is narrower than programs with multiple transfer partners, but for anyone willing to build Alaska miles intentionally, the 8-13 cents per mile value on JAL business class to Japan is extraordinarily difficult to beat.
